# Renal Anatomy And Physiology # Introduction The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs responsible for maintaining systemic homeostasis.  Their key functions include filtration and waste excretion, sodium and water balance, electrolyte and acid-base handling, and various endocrine roles (eg, vitamin D activation).  This review explores structural and functional characteristics of the kidney, from its embryologic development to the molecular mechanisms underlying filtration and reabsorption.  Endocrine functions are discussed in separate articles. # Embryology and gross morphology ## Embryology The definitive kidney, or metanephros, originates from the intermediate mesoderm.  Its development proceeds through a series of stages (pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros) during the fourth week of embryologic development.  The metanephros arises from the reciprocal interaction between the ureteric bud (which forms the collecting system) and the metanephric mesenchyme (which differentiates into nephrons) ((Figure 1)). ## Gross morphology Each adult kidney sits within the retroperitoneal space ((Figure 2)), shielded by a fibrous renal capsule and surrounded by perirenal fat.  This fatty cushion provides both mechanical protection and thermal insulation.  Each kidney receives blood flow from its respective renal artery and is drained by the renal veins.  The left renal vein is longer, making the left kidney preferred for renal transplant because the greater length simplifies the surgical procedure ((Figure 3)). Internally, the kidney can be divided into 2 primary regions ((Figure 4)): - **Renal cortex**:  This outer granular layer contains glomeruli and most metabolically active regions of the nephron (eg, early proximal tubule) with a rich vascular network. - **Renal medulla**:  This inner region contains renal pyramids and houses the loops of Henle, vasa recta, and collecting ducts.  Each pyramid terminates at a renal papilla, which projects into a minor calyx.  The renal papillae serve as the exit points where collecting ducts converge to drain urine into the minor calyces, which join to form major calyces that in turn converge into the renal pelvis. Some individuals are born with a solitary functioning kidney, as in the case of unilateral renal agenesis (failure of the ureteric bud to develop).  Although most of these people remain asymptomatic due to compensatory hyperfiltration by the remaining kidney, they face an elevated risk for chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to hyperfiltration injury. # The nephron The nephron is the fundamental functional unit of the kidney, responsible for transforming filtered blood (the filtrate) into urine ((Figure 5)).  Each kidney contains approximately 1 million nephrons, each of which consists of a renal corpuscle (site of filtrate formation) and tubule (site of filtrate refinement). ## Renal corpuscle: Filtrate formation The renal corpuscle forms the kidney's filtration apparatus ((Figure 6)) and consists of: - **Glomerulus**:  A specialized capillary network supplied by the afferent arteriole. - **Bowman capsule**:  A double-walled epithelial structure enclosing the glomerulus, consisting of simple squamous epithelium (parietal layer) and specialized podocytes with interdigitating foot processes connected by slit diaphragms (visceral layer) interspersed by proteins (eg, nephrin, podocin). Within the renal corpuscle, blood is filtered through the glomerular capillaries into the Bowman space (confined space within the capsule), forming the filtrate that ultimately becomes urine.  The filtration occurs across the **glomerular filtration barrier**, which progressively increases in selectivity (based on particle size) as substances pass through its 3 layers: - **Fenestrated endothelium**:  Fenestrated endothelium forms the innermost layer of the glomerular capillaries, permitting the passage of many plasma components through pores (70-100 nm in diameter).  Fluid, dissolved solutes, and plasma proteins are allowed through, whereas blood cells are not. - **Glomerular basement membrane (GBM)**:  This middle layer is composed of type IV collagen and heparan sulfate, serving as the most significant physical barrier.  The GBM prevents entry of molecules >40-50 nm. - **Podocyte foot processes**:  These processes form the outermost layer and contain small slit diaphragms (25-60 nm in diameter) that restrict the passage of proteins larger than approximately 70 kDa. In addition to the size barriers, **negatively charged glycoproteins** in all 3 layers add an electrostatic filter that repels larger, negatively charged solutes (eg, albumin) while not affecting small solutes (eg, electrolytes).  This intricate filtration system comprising physical and electrochemical barriers ensures that essential plasma proteins remain in circulation while waste products, electrolytes, and excess fluid are filtered ((Figure 7)). ## Renal tubules: Filtrate refinement Once the glomerular filtrate is formed, it enters the tubular system, where its composition is adjusted through tubular reabsorption (movement of substances from tubular lumen to blood) and secretion (movement from blood to tubular lumen).  The result—the net sum of filtration, reabsorption, and secretion—is excretion, the forming of the final urine.  The functionally distinct tubular segments include: - **Proximal convoluted tubule** (PCT) - Lined by cuboidal epithelial cells with a prominent brush border and abundant mitochondria, optimizing it for extensive solute reabsorption. - Reabsorbs 65%-70% of filtered Na⁺ (eg, via Na+/H+ exchangers), in addition to glucose (via sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 \[SGLT-2\] ((Figure 8))), bicarbonate ((Figure 9)), phosphate (regulated by parathyroid hormone), and Ca2+. - Secretes organic anions (eg, penicillin) via organic anion transporters and reabsorbs uric acid.  Both functions are inhibited by probenecid, a gout medication with a uricosuric effect (probenecid should be avoided in patients taking penicillin) ((Figure 10)). - Renal glucose handling follows a titration curve:  At plasma glucose <200 mg/dL, nearly all filtered glucose is reabsorbed.  Beyond the transport maximum, excess glucose spills into urine (glucosuria) ((Figure 11)). - **Loop of Henle** - Descending limb:  Passively reabsorbs water, concentrating tubular fluid. - Thick ascending limb (TAL):  Impermeable to water, it actively transports Na+, K+, and Cl− into the medullary interstitium via Na+\-K+\-2Cl− cotransporters.  This creates a medullary concentration gradient, allowing water reabsorption and urine concentration (discussed later). - Reabsorbs Mg2+ and Ca2+ via paracellular pathways. - **Distal convoluted tubule** (DCT) - This segment adjusts sodium and calcium concentrations (eg, via Na+\-Cl− cotransporters) under regulation by parathyroid hormone. - **Collecting duct** (CD) - The nephron's final segment, the CD, determines urine concentration and composition. - Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) regulates water reabsorption via aquaporin-2 channels, concentrating urine when present and allowing dilution in its absence ((Figure 12)). - Principal cells secrete K+ (via ROMK channels) and reabsorb Na+ (via ENaC), modulated by aldosterone.  Intercalated cells maintain acid-base balance by secreting H+ (via H+\-ATPase) and modulating bicarbonate transport.  Both are regulated by aldosterone ((Figure 13)). - Urea passively diffuses out of the inner medullary CD, contributing to the medullary osmotic gradient. The following is a summary of electrolyte handling through the tubular segments: - Sodium:  Reabsorbed in PCT (65%), TAL (25%), and DCT/CD (10%). - Potassium:  Reabsorbed in PCT/TAL; secreted in CD (regulated by aldosterone). - Phosphate:  Reabsorbed in PCT (inhibited by parathyroid hormone). - Calcium:  Reabsorbed in PCT (60%), TAL (20%), and DCT (20%). - Magnesium:  Primarily reabsorbed in TAL (70%). There are 2 types of nephrons specialized for different purposes.  **Cortical nephrons** make up the majority of nephrons and are optimized for solute reabsorption (ie, contain short loops of Henle) into peritubular capillaries.  **Juxtamedullary nephrons** extend deep into the medulla and are therefore critical for concentrating urine through the countercurrent multiplication system. The countercurrent multiplication system ((Figure 14)) establishes a **medullary concentration gradient** in the renal medulla to facilitate water reabsorption.  It relies on the unique structure of the loop of Henle.  The descending limb is permeable to water but not solutes; this allows water to leave the tubules, increasing tubular fluid osmolarity.  In contrast, the ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively transports sodium, potassium, and chloride into the medullary interstitium, reducing tubular fluid osmolarity while increasing medullary solute concentration.  This countercurrent flow amplifies the osmotic gradient, which is essential for the CD to reabsorb water under the influence of ADH, ultimately concentrating the urine.  The vasa recta, a specialized capillary network, helps maintain this gradient by preventing the washout of solutes from the medulla. # Vascular architecture Blood enters the kidneys via the renal artery, which divides into interlobar arteries, then arcuate arteries, and, finally, cortical radial arteries.  These give rise to afferent arterioles, forming the glomerular capillary network.  After blood is filtered through the glomerulus, it exits via the efferent arterioles, forming peritubular capillaries (in cortical nephrons) or the vasa recta (in juxtamedullary nephrons) ((Figure 15)).  The blood is finally collected from the peritubular network into cortical radial veins, which coalesce into arcuate veins, then interlobar veins, and, finally, the renal vein. The renal cortex receives approximately 90%-95% of renal blood flow, whereas the renal medulla receives the remaining 5%-10%.  This makes the medulla very sensitive to hypoxia, as demonstrated by the injury pattern seen in ischemic acute tubular necrosis, with the outer medullary cells being most affected ((Figure 16)). # Glomerular filtration ## Net filtration pressure The net filtration pressure, which governs fluid movement across the glomerular filtration barrier, is a result of pressure gradients formed by Starling forces and is calculated by subtracting the oncotic pressure gradient from the hydrostatic pressure gradient (ie, net filtration pressure = \[Pc − Pi\] − \[πc − πi\]) ((Figure 17)): - The hydrostatic pressure gradient (Pc − Pi) is the difference between the hydrostatic pressures in the intraglomerular capillaries and the Bowman space.  Hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries is higher than that in the Bowman space and provides the driving force for fluid efflux from the capillaries. - The oncotic pressure gradient (πc − πi) is the difference between the oncotic pressures in the intraglomerular capillaries and the Bowman space.  Oncotic pressure is driven chiefly by large plasma proteins (eg, albumin), which do not freely filter across the glomerular capillary basement membrane due to both size and charge barriers.  The high oncotic pressure in the capillaries counteracts the capillary hydrostatic pressure and decreases net fluid efflux from the capillaries. ## Renal clearance and renal plasma flow Renal **clearance** is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a given substance by the kidneys per unit time (usually expressed in mL/min).  It reflects the kidney's efficiency in removing a substance from the bloodstream.  Renal clearance of any substance (S) can be calculated as:

Clearance = (\[Urine concentration of S\] × \[Urine flow rate\]) / (Plasma concentration of S)

Renal clearance can vary from 0 to >600 mL/min, depending on the substance.  For example, under normal physiologic conditions, clearance of albumin and glucose is 0 (albumin is not filtered; glucose is filtered and then completely reabsorbed).  In contrast, maximum clearance is demonstrated by **para-aminohippurate** (PAH), which is freely filtered in the glomerulus and also actively secreted in the proximal tubule (ie, tubular fluid concentration increases along the nephron segments ((Figure 18))).  PAH is nearly completely cleared in 1 renal pass, and its clearance therefore approximates the **renal plasma flow** (RPF), which is the volume of plasma passing through the kidney per unit of time (approximately 625 mL/min). In contrast to PAH clearance, inulin clearance, described in the next section, is the gold standard for measuring the glomerular filtration rate ((Figure 19)). ## Glomerular filtration rate The **glomerular filtration rate** (GFR) represents the volume of plasma filtered per minute, typically 90-120 mL/min in healthy adults.  GFR represents the sum of filtration rates across all nephrons and is most accurately measured through **inulin clearance**.  Inulin, an exogenous substance, is an ideal marker because it is freely filtered by the glomerulus and not reabsorbed, secreted, or metabolized by the renal tubules.  As a result, the amount of filtered inulin exactly equals the amount excreted in urine.  However, this method is labor intensive, requiring continuous infusion and multiple blood and urine samples, limiting its clinical use. In clinical practice, GFR is typically estimated using the serum concentration of **creatinine**, a waste product generated during muscle metabolism of creatine.  Creatinine is produced at a relatively constant rate proportional to muscle mass and is freely filtered by the glomerulus without being reabsorbed (and is only slightly secreted).  The **estimated GFR** (eGFR) is calculated using formulas (eg, CKD-EPI, MDRD) that incorporate serum creatinine alongside variables such as age, sex, and race. The relationship between serum creatinine and GFR is nonlinear.  A useful clinical rule is that each 50% reduction in GFR correlates with a doubling of serum creatinine.  For example, if a serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL corresponds to a GFR of 100 mL/min, a decline in GFR to 50 mL/min raises serum creatinine to 2.0 mg/dL.  Further reductions to 25, 12.5, and 6.25 mL/min would yield serum creatinine levels of 4.0, 8.0, and 16.0 mg/dL, respectively.  This curvilinear relationship means that in early kidney disease even minor increases in serum creatinine reflect substantial declines in GFR ((Figure 20)).  Consequently, serum creatinine alone is an insensitive marker for detecting early CKD, underscoring why GFR—rather than creatinine concentration alone—is used for CKD staging and management. ## Creatinine clearance Alternatively, **creatinine clearance** (CrCl) provides another approximation of GFR.  CrCl can be measured directly using a 24-hour urine creatinine collection or estimated using the Cockcroft-Gault formula (which incorporates age, weight, sex, and serum creatinine).  However, unlike inulin, a small fraction of creatinine is actively secreted by the proximal tubules, leading to an overestimation of GFR by approximately 10%-20% when using uncorrected CrCl.  Although this overestimation makes CrCl less suitable for precise CKD diagnosis and staging, it remains widely used for medication dosing adjustments because drug dosing studies and guidelines were historically developed using CrCl measurements. ## Advanced biomarkers Given that both eGFR and CrCl rely on serum creatinine, both have limitations in individuals with low muscle mass (eg, malnutrition, lower extremity amputation) or high- or low-protein diets.  In such cases, advanced biomarkers are helpful.  For instance, cystatin C, a small protein produced by all nucleated cells (ie, not affected by muscle mass or dietary protein) and freely filtered by the glomerulus, offers a more reliable biomarker. # Renal hemodynamics ## Renal blood flow and filtration fraction RPF (approximated by PAH clearance) can be used to calculate the following: - Renal blood flow (RBF):  Defined as the volume of whole blood (plasma plus blood cells) passing through the kidneys per unit time.  RBF = RPF/(1 − hematocrit).  RBF reflects overall renal perfusion (approximately 25% of cardiac output, or 1.25 L/min) and is influenced by systemic hemodynamics (eg, blood pressure, vascular resistance). - Filtration fraction (FF):  Expressed as the ratio of GFR to RPF.  It is the portion of RPF that is filtered across the glomerular capillaries.  Normally, FF is approximately 20%, meaning that 20% of the RBF is filtered.  The remaining 80% of the RBF exits the efferent arterioles and joins the peritubular capillary blood flood. ## Mechanisms regulating GFR and RBF Both GFR and RBF are influenced by the vascular tone of both the afferent and the efferent arterioles, as shown in the following table ((Table 1)). # Juxtaglomerular apparatus The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is a specialized structure located where the DCT contacts the afferent and efferent arterioles ((Figure 21)).  The JGA is critical for regulating RBF and glomerular filtration and consists of the following components: - **Macula densa**:  Chemoreceptor cells that sense sodium chloride (NaCl) concentration in the tubular fluid via Na+\-K+\-2Cl− transporters. - **Juxtaglomerular cells**:  Modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin in response to decreased blood pressure, reduced NaCl, or sympathetic stimulation. - **Extraglomerular mesangial cells**:  Cells that facilitate communication within the JGA through gap junctions, fine-tuning the feedback response. In addition to regulating RBF and GFR (discussed in the next section), the JGA also plays a key role in the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system** (RAAS) by releasing renin in response to a variety of renal stimuli, including reduced afferent arteriolar pressure, reduced sodium delivery, and increased sympathetic drive.  Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is then converted to angiotensin II by ACE.  Angiotensin II causes systemic vasoconstriction (increasing blood pressure), promotes aldosterone release (increasing blood volume), and stimulates thirst ((Figure 22)). # Regulation of renal blood flow ## Normal renal autoregulation Normally, the kidneys maintain **stable RBF and GFR** over a wide range of mean arterial pressures (MAPs) (80-180 mm Hg) ((Figure 23)).  This process, called renal autoregulation, is accomplished through dynamic adjustments in **afferent arteriole** resistance via the following mechanisms: - **Myogenic response**:  Rising arterial pressure stretches afferent arteriolar smooth muscle, triggering vasoconstriction (through opening of stretch-activated calcium channels).  This reduces blood flow into the glomerulus, preventing abrupt increases in glomerular pressure.  Conversely, dropping arterial pressure triggers afferent vasodilation, increasing RBF (and hence GFR). - **Tubuloglomerular feedback**:  Increased arterial pressure leads to higher filtration of NaCl, which is delivered to the macula densa.  This triggers the paracrine release of vasoconstrictors (eg, adenosine), causing afferent arteriole constriction to limit blood flow.  In contrast, as pressures drop, reduced NaCl delivery releases vasodilators (eg, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) to maintain RBF and GFR. ## Failure of renal autoregulation Under extreme deviations in MAP (<80 mm Hg or >180 mm Hg), renal blood flow autoregulation is unable to maintain stable RBF and GFR, as demonstrated in the following scenarios: - ↓↓ **MAP**:  Autoregulatory vasodilation is overwhelmed, unable to sufficiently elevate RBF and GFR.  Although compensatory prostaglandins (eg, prostaglandin E₂) dilate the afferent arteriole to preserve GFR, prolonged/severe hypotension exhausts this safeguard, causing prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI). - ↑↑ **MAP**:  Excessive pressure overwhelms autoregulatory vasoconstriction, exposing glomeruli to systemic hypertension.  This leads to hyperfiltration, glomerular damage, proteinuria, and inflammation (due to mesangial stretch), culminating in acute hypertensive nephrosclerosis. ## Clinical applications In addition to extreme MAP deviations, renal autoregulation can be disrupted in various clinical scenarios, including: - ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs):  These inhibit angiotensin II, which normally maintains GFR via efferent constriction during reduced MAP (eg, volume depletion).  As MAP decreases, patients on these drugs are prone to prerenal AKI due to afferent vasodilation ((Figure 24)).  However, in patients whose volume status is stable, these medications protect glomerular capillaries (eg, diabetic nephropathy) by reducing intraglomerular hypertension, slowing disease progression despite a minor GFR decline. - NSAIDs:  By inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis (eg, PGE₂), these medications prevent afferent arteriole dilation during hypoperfusion.  In states of low effective arterial blood volume (EABV) (eg, volume depletion, heart failure, cirrhosis), this causes unopposed vasoconstriction and AKI ((Figure 25)). - SGLT-2 inhibitors:  Blocking SGLT-2 in the proximal tubule reduces glucose and sodium reabsorption, increasing solute delivery to the macula densa.  This enhances tubuloglomerular feedback, causing afferent vasoconstriction, lowering intraglomerular pressure, and reducing hyperfiltration ((Figure 26)).  This renoprotective effect mimics those of ACE inhibitors and ARBs but targets afferent (rather than efferent) arterioles. - Nephrotoxic agents:  Intraarterial iodinated contrast may cause AKI via afferent vasoconstriction (and direct tubular toxicity), especially in CKD.  Calcineurin inhibitors (eg, tacrolimus) can also induce afferent vasoconstriction. - Hepatorenal syndrome:  Advanced cirrhosis leads to severe splanchnic vasodilation and reduced EABV.  Compensatory RAAS hyperactivity (from renal hypoperfusion) causes intense renal vasoconstriction, overwhelming autoregulatory mechanisms and impairing renal function. Beyond these acute disruptions, chronic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus also significantly impact renal autoregulation.  In chronic hypertension, prolonged high pressure shifts the autoregulatory range upward, making the kidneys reliant on high perfusion.  A sudden MAP drop (eg, from overtreatment) can cause AKI.  Diabetes mellitus promotes persistent afferent dilation (via multiple mechanisms), increasing glomerular hyperfiltration.  Over time, this damages the glomerular basement membrane, leading to proteinuria and nephropathy.  Both conditions impair perfusion stability, heightening AKI risk during hemodynamic stress. # Summary The kidneys maintain homeostasis through intricate filtration, reabsorption, and secretion mechanisms.  Cortical nephrons dominate solute reabsorption, whereas juxtamedullary nephrons establish the medullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent multiplication (allowing water reabsorption with concentration of urine). The glomerular filtration barrier combines size-selective (eg, glomerular basement membrane, podocytes) and charge-selective (ie, negatively charged glycoproteins) layers to exclude plasma proteins.  Tubular segments use specialized transporters to adjust filtrate composition, modulated by various hormones (eg, antidiuretic hormone, aldosterone). Renal hemodynamics are autoregulated via myogenic responses and tubuloglomerular feedback, maintaining the glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow across a wide range of mean arterial pressures (80-180 mm Hg).  Clinical biomarkers (eg, creatinine, cystatin C) and clearance techniques (eg, inulin clearance) quantify renal function.  Pharmacologic agents (eg, ACE inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors) target glomerular pressure to mitigate hyperfiltration injury.  Disrupted autoregulation (eg, NSAIDs, hypotension) precipitates acute kidney injury, underscoring the kidney's vulnerability to hemodynamic perturbations. ​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌

# Neuroanatomy: Cortical Lobe Function, Basic Tracts, Arterial Anatomy, And Neurolocalization

# Introduction

Neuroanatomy provides the foundation for understanding the functional organization of the central nervous system (CNS).  The brain and spinal cord contain a network of neural tracts responsible for transmitting motor, sensory, and autonomic information.  Damage to these pathways results in characteristic clinical deficits, which allows for localization of neurological lesions based on the tracts involved.  This article reviews the basic organization of cortical lobes and key tracts in the CNS and describes how lesions at different levels lead to specific patterns of deficits, concluding with a discussion of arterial anatomy and stroke localization.

# Cortical lobes:  Overview

Each cerebral lobe is specialized for distinct functions, with significant interconnectivity between regions ((Figure 1)).  Damage to any area can lead to characteristic clinical syndromes, depending on the specific lobe involved.  The right and left hemispheres also have specialized functions based upon which is considered the "dominant" hemisphere, which can impact how a lesion may present.  Almost 90% of right-handed patients and 60% of left-handed patients have a **left hemispheric dominance**.  In general, hemispheric control is split:

-   Dominant hemisphere (left) typically controls speech/language, reading, writing, and most arithmetic.
-   Nondominant hemisphere (right) is involved in visual/spatial analysis and attention.

# Frontal lobe

The frontal lobe ((Figure 2)) is responsible for several primary functions, including:

-   Voluntary motor control (starting from the primary motor cortex), including eye movements and the micturition reflex
-   Motor production of speech
-   Higher-order executive function (eg, planning, social behavior)

## Primary motor cortex

The primary motor cortex, also known as the **precentral gyrus**, controls voluntary movements via the corticospinal tract ((Figure 3)).  The **motor homunculus** is a representation of the body's musculature regions mapped onto the prefrontal cortex ((Figure 4)).  The medial portion corresponds with the lower extremities, whereas the lateral portion corresponds with the trunk and upper extremities; areas requiring fine motor control (eg, hands, face) occupy disproportionately large regions compared to areas such as the trunk or legs.

Damage to this area of the brain results in contralateral weakness or paralysis.  Because of the organization of the homunculus, lesions affecting specific areas of the motor cortex cause deficits in the corresponding body parts.  For example:

-   A lesion in the medial cortex results in contralateral leg weakness.
-   A lesion in the lateral cortex causes weakness in the contralateral face or arm.

## Broca area (eg, dominant frontal lobe)

Broca area is located adjacent to the primary motor cortex in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) of the dominant (left) frontal lobe ((Figure 5)).  This region is responsible for all communicative motor planning.  Lesions cause Broca aphasia, in which patients can comprehend and follow commands but are unable to verbalize or write properly (**expressive aphasia**) ((Figure 6)).  This may present with the following:

-   Very slow speech
-   Speech with very few words, usually nouns and verbs only
-   Speech that may be punctuated by pauses in between words as the patient attempts to verbalize each one
-   Variable ability to repeat words and phrases when asked
-   Frustration due to an awareness of expressive language dysfunction

## Prefrontal cortex

This area of the brain is involved in planning, decision-making, and behavior modulation.  Damage to his area often leads to executive dysfunction, social disinhibition, and impaired problem-solving.

## Frontal eye fields

This portion of the frontal lobe is responsible for voluntary control of eye movements.  Frontal eye fields send projections to the contralateral nucleus for CN VI (abducens) and structures in the pons (eg, paramedian pontine reticular formation \[PPRF\]) to allow for conjugate horizontal gaze in the opposite direction (eg, left frontal eye field will control eye movement to the right) ((Figure 7)).  Damage to this area causes a gaze preference, in which the patient looks toward the side of the lesion because of unopposed action from the working hemisphere.

## Frontal micturition center

This area of the medial frontal lobe controls voluntary cortical inhibition of the micturition reflex.  Damage can cause urinary incontinence.

# Parietal lobe

The parietal lobe is primarily involved in processing contralateral somatosensory information as well as in multisensory integration (including processing information, facilitating comprehension, and problem solving).  Damage can cause a wide range of complex signs and symptoms, depending on whether the dominant or nondominant side is affected.

## Primarily somatosensory cortex

The primary somatosensory cortex, also known as the postcentral gyrus, processes contralateral somatosensory information, such as touch, proprioception, and pain ((Figure 8)).  The **sensory homunculus** mirrors the motor homunculus but represents areas of the body receiving sensory input ((Figure 9)).  Like the motor homunculus, the medial portion corresponds with the lower extremities, whereas the lateral portion corresponds with the trunk and upper extremities while areas with greater sensory input (eg, hands, lips) occupy more cortical space.

-   Lesions result in contralateral sensory deficits.
-   Lesions may also cause the loss of multiple forms of higher-level sensory processing (ie, cortical sensory signs), including two-point discrimination, stereognosis (the ability to recognize an object only through touch), ability to perceive multiple stimuli at the same time (loss of this is called extinction), and/or graphesthesia (the ability to recognize numbers or letters traced on the palm).

## Nondominant parietal lobe (right)

The nondominant parietal lobe (typically the right) integrates visual and spatial information and is responsible for **spatial awareness and attention**.  Damage leads to **hemineglect**, where patients fail to recognize objects or body parts on the opposite side.  This can manifest as:

-   sensory neglect, which includes tactile, visual, and even auditory neglect.  It can be assessed with extinction testing (bilateral sensory stimulus experienced only on one side).  Patients may also have a construction apraxia (eg, inability to copy or perform simple line drawings).
-   motor-intentional neglect, which includes decreased spontaneous movement on the neglected side despite normal strength and use of the "incorrect" (ie, normal) arm when instructed to move the affected arm.  This may also present as a dressing apraxia (eg, difficulty in wearing clothes or only putting on one side).
-   conceptual neglect, which may include a lack of awareness or denial about the deficits (eg, anosognosia).  In severe cases, patients may even say that half of their body does not belong to them.

## Dominant parietal lobe (left)

The dominant parietal lobe plays a significant role in **processing language and math**.  Therefore, damage classically results in issues related to these higher-order functions.  For example, Gerstmann syndrome (from damage to the inferior parietal lobe) is characterized by the following:

-   Alexia (inability to read)
-   Agraphia (inability to write)
-   Acalculia (inability to solve mathematical calculations)
-   Finger agnosia (inability to identify individual fingers on the hand)
-   Left-right disorientation

## Arcuate fasciculus

The arcuate fasciculus is the white matter tract in the parietal lobe that connects Broca and Wernicke areas.  Lesions usually cause a **conduction aphasia** ((Figure 10)), which is characterized by the following:

-   Phonemic paraphasic errors (ie, replacing words that sound similar to intended words \[eg, "show" vs "know," "right" vs "night"\])
-   Impaired repetition
-   Impaired naming of objects
-   Frequent attempts at correction

# Temporal lobe

The temporal lobe is primarily involved in hearing/language comprehension and many of its structures (eg, hippocampus, amygdalae) are also a critical component of the limbic system, which is involved in memory formation and emotional regulation.

## Wernicke area (eg, dominant temporal lobe)

Wernicke area (Brodmann area 22) is located in the caudal superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (left) temporal lobe and is involved in hearing and language comprehension.  Lesions in Wernicke area cause Wernicke aphasia (eg, **receptive aphasia**) ((Figure 11)), which is characterized by the following:

-   Fluent, well-articulated, but nonsensical speech (eg, "word salad")
-   Lack of language comprehension (eg, difficulty comprehending and following commands)
-   Lack of insight of the deficits

## Hippocampus

The hippocampus, along with other medial temporal lobe structures, are critical for forming new memories.  Damage to this area results in anterograde amnesia.

# Occipital lobe

## Visual pathway

The occipital cortex is primarily responsible for processing incoming visual information.  The visual pathway leads to the occipital lobe and passes through many structures along the way to convey information from the retina ((Figure 12)).

Visual information from the temporal visual field of the ipsilateral eye will be conveyed through the following:

1.  Ipsilateral nasal hemiretina (light that enters the eye forms an image on the retina that is inverted and reversed).
2.  Ipsilateral optic nerve, which transmits information from one eye.
3.  Optic chiasm.  In the optic chiasm, fibers from the temporal visual fields (eg, bilateral nasal retinas) cross, whereas fibers from the nasal visual fields do NOT cross and instead travel along the same side of the brain for the rest of the pathway; this occurs so that the hemi-visual fields from both eyes are processed in the same, contralateral hemisphere of the brain.
4.  Contralateral optic tract.  After the optic chiasm, information from the binocular visual fields travels together in the contralateral optic tract.
5.  Contralateral lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
6.  Contralateral optic radiations.  The inferior optic radiations carry information from the superior visual field through the temporal lobe (Meyer loop), and the superior optic radiations carry information from the inferior visual field through the parietal lobe.
7.  Contralateral primary visual cortex, which is located in the occipital lobe.

Because of how fibers travel at the intersection of the optic chiasm, lesions posterior to the optic chiasm cause visual field defects that are the same in both eyes (ie, homonymous) and impact the contralateral visual field ((Figure 13)).

## Primary visual cortex

The primary visual cortex (striate cortex) is located in the occipital lobe and is where visual information is relayed from the eyes.  Lesions here cause **contralateral homonymous hemianopia**—a visual field defect on the opposite side of the lesion in both eyes.  Patients may also have associated anosognosia (lack of awareness of their condition) and confabulation (the unintentional generation of fabricated information to fill in gaps) due to the inability of the visual cortex to communicate with areas of the brain that conduct higher-order sensory integration and speech-language processing.

## Occipital association cortices

After visual information is received in the occipital cortex, it is relayed along distinct pathways to association cortices for higher-order processing ((Figure 14)).

-   The ventral pathways (P pathway) project to the occipitotemporal association cortex for identification of letters, colors, shapes, and faces (ie, "What is it?").  Damage to this area can lead to difficulty identifying or using objects.
-   The dorsal pathways (M pathway) project to the parieto-occipital association cortex for processing of motion and spatial relationships (ie, "Where is it?").  Bilateral damage to the parieto-occipital association cortices (usually due to systemic hypotension causing watershed ischemia) leads to Balint syndrome, which is characterized by optic ataxia (eg, difficulty localizing objects in space), ocular apraxia (eg, difficulty tracking objects), and/or simultanagnosia (eg, inability to understand complex visual scenes as a whole).

# Basal ganglia and thalamus

The basal ganglia and thalamus make up the deep gray nuclei in the cerebral hemispheres.  The basal ganglia (Figure 15)) is involved in regulating motor control ((Figure 16)) and is made up of several structures:

-   The **caudate nucleus** and **putamen** together make up the **striatum**, which is critical for movement control and coordination along with behavioral regulation.  The caudate nucleus is a curved or C-shaped structure in its complete form.  The head of the caudate can be identified in the inferolateral walls of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles.
-   The **subthalamic nucleus** is a lens-shaped structure located ventral (inferior) to the thalamus, dorsal (superior) to the substantia nigra, and medial to the internal capsule.  It plays an important role in the modulation of basal ganglia output.
-   The **globus pallidus** and substantia nigra (part of the midbrain) regulate movement.

Lesions in the basal ganglia typically cause a variety of movement disorders (eg, Parkinson disease, Huntington disease, hemiballismus).  The thalamus is a relay center for motor and sensory tracts and also is involved in the regulation of sleep and consciousness; lesions most commonly cause sensory loss or thalamic pain.

# Cerebellum

The cerebellum is the largest structure in the posterior fossa and consists of the vermis at the midline and 2 cerebellar hemispheres ((Figure 17)).

-   The cerebellar **hemispheres** are responsible primarily for motor planning and coordination of the ipsilateral extremities via their connections with the lateral descending motor systems (eg, lateral corticospinal tract, rubrospinal tract).  Lesions affect the cerebellar hemisphere typically result in the ipsilateral symptoms of dysdiadochokinesia (impaired, rapid alternating movements), limb dysmetria (overshoot/undershoot during targeted movement), and intention tremor (tremor during targeted movement).
-   The cerebellar **vermis** modulates axial/truncal posture and coordination via connections with the medial descending motor systems (eg, anterior corticospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, and tectospinal tracts).  Lesions in this region result in truncal ataxia (eg, wide-based, unsteady gait).  Vertigo and nystagmus may also occur due to disruption of the inferior vermis and the flocculonodular lobe.

# Major motor pathways

## Corticospinal tract (pyramidal tract)

The corticospinal tract is the primary pathway for voluntary motor control, particularly fine motor movements ((Figure 18)).

-   Upper motor neuron (UMN) fibers originate in the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus.
-   Fibers descend through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncles of the midbrain, pons, and medullary pyramids.
-   At the caudal medulla, most of the fibers decussate (cross) and continue as the lateral corticospinal tract in the contralateral spinal cord.
-   The lateral corticospinal tract fibers synapse on lower motor neurons (LMNs) in the anterior horn of the spinal cord, which innervate the limb muscles.

Following this pathway can help with lesion localization.

-   Lesions **above the decussation** (eg, cortex, internal capsule, brainstem) will produce contralateral motor deficits.
-   Lesions **below the decussation** (eg, spinal cord) will cause ipsilateral motor deficits.

In addition, patients may show different signs depending on whether the UMN or LMN is affected.  UMN injury, which occurs anywhere proximal to the anterior horn, can cause weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and the upgoing plantar reflexes.  LMN injuries, seen in lesions at the anterior horn cells or peripheral nerves, can cause flaccid paralysis, atrophy, fasciculations, and hyporeflexia.

## Corticobulbar tract

The corticobulbar tract controls **motor output to cranial nerves** (CNs) responsible for movements of the **face, head, and neck**.  Similar to what occurs in the corticospinal tract, the UMNs arise from the primary motor cortex.  These neurons descend similarly to the corticospinal tract but terminate in the brainstem at the level of the motor nuclei of CNs.

Bilateral innervation occurs for most CNs, except for the lower face (CN VII) and tongue (CN XII), which receive predominantly contralateral input.  This is clinically relevant as unilateral lesions in these pathways produce **contralateral** deficits:

-   Lesions in the UMN of the lower face produce contralateral deficits in lower facial muscles (lower face droop) due to the predominant contralateral innervation of the lower half of the face (see article on "Facial palsy").
-   Tongue deviation **toward** the side of the lesion occurs with hypoglossal (CN XII) involvement.

# Major sensory pathways

## Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway

The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway (DCML) transmits **proprioception, vibration sense, and fine touch** from the body to the brain ((Figure 19)).

-   First-order neurons from the sensory receptors of the skin, joints, and muscles ascend ipsilaterally in the **dorsal columns** of the spinal cord (fasciculus gracilis for lower body, fasciculus cuneatus for upper body).  The cell bodies of these first-order neurons are located in the dorsal root ganglia.
-   These neurons travel up the spinal cord and synapse in the gracile and cuneate nuclei in the medulla.  The second-order neurons decussate in the medulla and ascend as the **medial lemniscus** and synapse in ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus.
-   Third-order neurons project to the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus.
-   As with the corticospinal tract, clinical findings may help with localization of the lesion:
-   Lesions **above the decussation** (eg, brainstem, thalamus, cortex) produce contralateral deficits in proprioception, vibration, and fine touch.
-   Lesions **below the decussation** (eg, spinal cord) result in ipsilateral deficits.

Sensory ataxia causing proprioception issues can be distinguished from cerebellar ataxia with the **Romberg test**.  The maneuver is executed by first instructing the patient to stand with the feet close together, arms to the sides, and eyes open, and observing for unsteadiness, which indicates some form of ataxia (cerebellar or sensory).  To differentiate sensory from cerebellar ataxia, the patient is then asked to close the eyes while maintaining the aforementioned posture, which removes visual input and forces the patient to rely on input from proprioceptive receptors in the trunk and extremities for posture maintenance.  Failure to maintain this posture with the eyes closed (positive Romberg sign) indicates sensory ataxia, which may be due to lesions in the dorsal column or peripheral nerves (eg, tabes dorsalis).  Patients with ataxia who show little or no change in their unsteadiness with their eyes closed (ie, ataxia with a negative Romberg sign) likely have cerebellar ataxia due to impaired motor coordination, typically evaluated with rapid alternating movements, finger-to-nose testing, and heel-to-shin testing.  

## Spinothalamic (anterolateral) tract

The spinothalamic tract transmits **pain, temperature, and crude touch** ((Figure 20)).

-   First-order neurons synapse from the sensory receptors of the skin, joints, and muscles in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
-   Second-order neurons briefly **ascend 1-2 spinal levels** and decussate in the anterior white commissure and ascend contralaterally in the anterolateral columns.
-   These fibers project to the thalamus (ventral posterolateral nucleus) and eventually to the primary somatosensory cortex.
-   Localizing lesions of the spinothalamic tract:
-   Lesions **at the spinal cord level** will produce ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion.
-   Lesions **above spinal level, brainstem, or higher** will cause contralateral deficits (starting 1-2 levels below the lesion) due to the decussation in the spinal cord
-   Lesions of the **anterior white commissure (eg, central cord syndrome, syringomyelia)** causes bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in a "cape-like" distribution, with sparing of fine touch and proprioception (as the dorsal columns remain intact)

# Brainstem

The brainstem contains important tracts and nuclei that come from its 3 major areas:  the midbrain, the pons, and the medulla.  Each portion of the brainstem has distinct functions that play a role in critical regulation of the body as well as in relaying motor and sensory information.

Additionally, the CNs exit the brainstem at particular points ((Figure 21)); lesions of the CNs can cause specific deficits that can be helpful for localization ((Table 1)).  Because most CNs (other than CNs II & IV) do not decussate while most of the body's motor and sensory fibers cross the midline in the medulla, brainstem pathology is characterized by ipsilateral CN deficits accompanied by contralateral hemiparesis or hemisensory loss (ie, crossed signs).

## Midbrain

The midbrain is the most rostral portion of the brainstem.  Key structures in the midbrain include:

-   Corticospinal and corticobulbar pathways for motor control
-   Pretectal structures (eg, the colliculi), which help control and coordinate vertical gaze and the pupillary light reflex ((Figure 22))
-   CN III (oculomotor) and CN IV (trochlear), which are involved in eye movements
-   Red nucleus, which is involved in motor coordination (for more information, see article on increased intracranial pressure)
-   Substantia nigra, which contains dopamine-producing neurons and is involved in movement coordination with the structures of the basal ganglia
-   Reticular formation, which is involved in regulation of consciousness

Specific syndromes that occur in the midbrain and reflect its function include:

-   **Weber syndrome** ((Figure 23)):  This is often caused by a midbrain infarction due to occlusion of mesencephalic branches of the posterior cerebral artery or perforating arteries of the basilar bifurcation.  It can present with:
    -   ipsilateral CN III dysfunction (eg, ptosis, impaired pupil constriction, down-and-out eye, diplopia).
    -   contralateral face, arm, and leg weakness.  Facial weakness impacts only the lower face, which is consistent with an upper motor neuron pattern.
    -   contralateral parkinsonism,
-   **Parinaud syndrome**:  This is usually caused by a pineal gland tumor that pushes on the dorsal midbrain.  It presents with:
    -   limitation of upward gaze with downward gaze preference (ie, setting-sun sign) due to compression of the vertical gaze center (medial longitudinal fasciculus).
    -   light-near dissociation (ie, pseudo–Argyll Robertson pupil):  pupils reactive to accommodation but not to light due to disruption of dorsal optic tract fibers traveling to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei.
    -   convergence retraction nystagmus (ie, nystagmus and retraction of the globe with upward gaze) and bilateral eyelid retraction (ie, Collier sign) due to disruption of the inhibitory fibers to the nucleus of CN III (affecting the rectus muscles and levator palpebrae).
    -   ataxia due to compression of the superior cerebellar peduncle.

## Pons

The pons is located between the medulla and midbrain.  Key structures in the pons include the following:

-   Pontine respiratory center
-   Corticospinal and corticobulbar pathways for motor control
-   Centers for control of conjugate horizontal gaze ((Figure 24))
-   CNs V (trigeminal), VI (abducens), VII (facial), and VIII (vestibulocochlear), all of which exit at the level of the pons

A syndrome that occurs in the pons and reflects its function is **locked-in syndrome** ((Figure 25)).  This syndrome is classically caused by occlusion of the basilar artery or by central pontine myelinolysis (eg, rapid correction of hyponatremia), which leads to dysfunction of the bilateral ventral pons.  It is characterized by:

-   absent voluntary motor function of the limbs (quadriplegia) and oral structures (loss of speech) due to destruction of the bilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar pathways, which prevent the CNs or the limbs from receiving cortical input.
-   absent horizontal eye movements because coordinated conjugate gaze is controlled in the pons; however, vertical eye movements and eyelid elevation are preserved because they are controlled in the rostral midbrain.
-   preserved consciousness because the midbrain reticular formation is spared.  Behavioral arousal and sleep-wake cycles are also preserved because the diencephalon–upper brainstem arousal systems are unaffected.
-   preserved sensation because sensory pathways are not affected, and preserved brainstem and spinal reflexes because they do not require cortical input.

**Internuclear ophthalmoplegia** is a disorder of impaired horizontal gaze caused by damage to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).  The frontal eye field initiates horizontal gaze through the contralateral abducens (CN VI) nucleus, which communicates with the ipsilateral oculomotor (CN III) nucleus by way of the MLF.  This allows for simultaneous activation of the lateral rectus muscle in the contralateral eye (abduction) and the medial rectus muscle in the ipsilateral eye (adduction), resulting in coordinated conjugate horizontal gaze.  Unilateral MLF lesions typically occur in older patients with lacunar strokes in the dorsal pons or midbrain (pontine artery distribution) and result in impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye during horizontal gaze, causing diplopia.  Abduction in the contralateral eye is preserved (but often with gaze-evoked nystagmus).  The pathways for convergence and the pupillary light reflex bypass the MLF lesion, so these reflexes are generally preserved.

## Medulla

The medulla is the most caudal portion of the brainstem.  Key structures in the medulla include:

-   Critical centers for respiratory and cardiac control
-   Decussation of the pyramids, which is where the somatosensory and motor tracts from the body cross
-   Inferior cerebellar peduncles
-   CNs IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (spinal accessory), and XII (hypoglossal), all of which exit here

Specific syndromes that occur in the medulla and reflect its function include:

-   **Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome)** (Figure 26)), usually caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or the vertebral artery, leading to:
    -   Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the body (spinothalamic tract)
    -   Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature of the face (spinal trigeminal nucleus)
    -   Vertigo without hearing loss (vestibular nucleus for CN VIII)
    -   Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (descending sympathetic nervous system fibers)
    -   Bulbar weakness causing dysphagia, hoarseness (CNs IX & X or nucleus ambiguus)
    -   Tongue weakness in which, on tongue protrusion, the strong side "pushes" the tongue toward the weak side (CN XII) (sometimes remembered as "licking your wounds")
    -   Ipsilateral cerebellar signs (inferior cerebellar peduncle)
-   **Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome)** ((Figure 27)), usually resulting from infarction of the anterior spinal artery and affecting the corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).  Symptoms include:
    -   Contralateral hemiparesis
    -   Contralateral loss of proprioception/vibration
    -   Ipsilateral tongue weakness

# Arterial anatomy of the brain and stroke localization

The brain's arterial supply ((Figure 28)) is divided into **anterior circulation** (via the internal carotid arteries) and **posterior circulation** (via the vertebrobasilar system \[(Figure 29)).  Together, they form the circle of Willis, which is somewhat protective against ischemic injury because it provides a potential alternate pathway for cerebral arterial blood flow ((Figure 30)).

## Middle cerebral artery

The middle cerebral artery (MCA) arises from the internal carotid artery and supplies posterior portions of the frontal lobe, anterior portions of the parietal lobe, and a large area of the temporal lobe.  This includes the **primary motor and sensory cortices**; the **upper extremity and face** are primarily affected in MCA strokes because the MCA supplies the lateral portions of the primary motor and somatosensory cortices ((Figure 31)).  MCA infarcts characteristically lead to:

-   contralateral hemiparesis of the face and upper limb due to infarction of the primary motor cortex.
-   contralateral sensory loss of the face and upper limb due to infarction of the primary somatosensory cortex.
-   contralateral homonymous hemianopia or homonymous quadrantanopia without macular sparing due to involvement of the upper and/or lower limbs of the optic radiations.
-   gaze deviation due to disruption of the frontal eye field (looking toward the lesion).
-   aphasia, which occurs with lesions to the dominant (usually left) hemisphere.  This can be Broca or Wernicke aphasia (or both) depending on which structures are affected; infarcts of the superior division of the MCA usually cause a Broca aphasia, whereas infarcts of the inferior division cause a Wernicke aphasia.
-   contralateral neglect due to disruption of the nondominant (usually right) parietal cortex.

## Anterior cerebral artery

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) also arises from the internal carotid artery and supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes.  This includes the **medial portions of the primary motor and sensory cortices**, which explains why the **lower extremities** are primarily affected by ACA strokes ((Figure 32)).  The anterior communicating artery (ACom) provides an anastomotic pathway between the bilateral anterior cerebral arteries, which may limit the severity of infarction if occlusion occurs proximal to the ACom.  Therefore, in a symptomatic ACA stroke, it is more likely that the obstruction is located distal to the origin of the ACom, where collateral blood flow does not occur.  ACA infarcts characteristically lead to the following:

-   Contralateral hemiparesis of the lower extremity due to infarction of the medial portion of the primary motor cortex
-   Contralateral sensory loss of the lower extremity due to infarction of the medial portion of the primary somatosensory cortex
-   Urinary incontinence due to impairment of the frontal micturition center
-   Symptoms of disruption of the prefrontal cortex, including:
    -   Abulia (lack of will or initiation)
    -   Apraxia (inability to carry out complex motions despite normal motor function)
    -   Emotional disturbances, executive dysfunction, flat affect
    -   Appearance of primitive reflexes:  most often the grasp reflex (finger flexion around an object placed in the palm)

## Posterior cerebral artery

The posterior cerebral artery (PCA) arises from the basilar artery and supplies the occipital lobe, parts of the parietal and temporal lobes, and the thalamus.  PCA infarcts characteristically lead to:

-   contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (vision loss in the same visual field of both eyes).  The macula is often spared due to collateral circulation from the middle cerebral artery.
-   contralateral complete hemisensory loss due to lateral thalamic dysfunction.
-   dysfunction of cortical association areas (eg, alexia, visual agnosia, prosopagnosia, and/or neglect).

## Vertebral and basilar arteries (posterior circulation)

The bilateral vertebral arteries join at the junction between the medulla and pons, forming the basilar artery.  The vertebral arteries supply the medulla, while the basilar artery supplies the upper brainstem (eg, midbrain, pons) and the cerebellum.  Infarcts of the posterior circulation characteristically lead to:

-   vertigo, which may be the presenting symptom of a posterior circulation stroke, especially in association with other neurologic signs/symptoms.
-   lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, most commonly seen with strokes in the intracranial vertebral artery distribution due to occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery.
-   various other brainstem syndromes (see section above on the brainstem).

## Small perforating arteries

Small perforating arteries (eg, lenticulostriate arteries) branch off the larger arteries; infarction of these can lead to lacunar infarcts that affect the deep subcortical structures ((Figure 33)).  The primary causes are thought to be lipohyalinosis (vascular wall hyaline thickening, collagenous sclerosis, and mural foamy macrophage accumulation) and microatheromas (atherosclerotic buildup of lipid-laden macrophages in the intima).  The deep penetrating arteries are quite small and therefore most susceptible to hypertension-related vascular disease, the most important risk factor for lacunar stroke.  Each of these has a characteristic clinical presentation if affected:

-   **Pure motor stroke**:  Patients with a stroke in the posterior limb of the internal capsule often have pure motor deficits, affecting the contralateral arm, leg, and lower face with UMN signs (eg, clasp-knife spasticity \[initial resistance to passive flexion followed by a sudden release of resistance\], hyperreflexia, and an upgoing plantar reflex).
-   **Pure sensory stroke**:  This usually occurs with lesions in the ventroposterolateral or ventroposteromedial thalamus, causing contralateral sensory loss.  Patients initially present with numbness but can subsequently develop burning pain, referred to as thalamic pain syndrome.  The pain is classically exacerbated by light touch (allodynia) but can be triggered by other sensory modalities (eg, sound, taste).
-   **Sensorimotor syndrome**:  Infarction of both the posterior limb of the internal capsule and thalamus can lead to sensorimotor syndrome, in which patients have contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss.
-   **Dysarthria–clumsy hand syndrome**:  This presents as dysarthria and dysphagia with clumsiness of one hand and occurs due to stroke in the anterior limb of the internal capsule and/or basal pons.
-   **Ataxia-hemiparesis**:  This presents as ipsilateral limb ataxia out of proportion to motor deficit, usually due to stroke in the anterior limb of the internal capsule and/or basal pons.
-   **Hemiballism**:  This a movement disorder characterized by wild, involuntary, large-amplitude, flinging movements involving the proximal limbs (eg, arm and/or leg) on one side of the body.  It usually occurs due to damage to the subthalamic nucleus, which is a lens-shaped structure located ventral (inferior) to the thalamus, dorsal (superior) to the substantia nigra, and medial to the internal capsule.

Mental status changes, seizures, CN deficits, and cortical signs are absent in lacunar strokes.

# Summary

Neuroanatomy forms the foundation for understanding the functional organization of the CNS, with the brain and spinal cord containing neural tracts that transmit motor, sensory, and autonomic information.  Damage to these pathways leads to specific clinical deficits, enabling localization of neurological lesions.  An understanding of the functions of the cortical lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital), basal ganglia, and cerebellum as well as of the major motor and sensory pathways and arterial anatomy helps link arterial supply to stroke localization and the resulting clinical syndromes associated with different vascular territories.

articles.title: Lymph Node Structure And Function
articles.markdown: # Lymph Node Structure And Function # Introduction Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped organs strategically located along lymphatic vessels throughout the body.  These specialized structures serve as filtration stations and immune response hubs, playing a crucial role in the body's defense against infections and surveillance of abnormal cells.  This article provides an overview of lymph node anatomy and physiology, with particular emphasis on their structural organization and functional significance within the immune system. # Structure and function Lymph nodes have a complex internal architecture that facilitates their immune functions ((Figure 1)).  An outer capsule composed of dense connective tissue encases and protects the node.  Underneath are trabeculae, which are internal fibrous extensions that project inward from the capsule, providing structural support and creating compartments for cellular organization.  Each lymph node contains a hilum, a concave region allowing passage of arterial and venous blood and containing efferent lymphatic vessels. Each node is organized into 3 distinct but interconnected regions:  cortex, paracortex, and medulla. ## Cortex The cortex is the outer region of the lymph node.  It primarily houses **B lymphocytes** and is organized into distinct structures: - **Primary follicles**:  Consist of spherical collections of **quiescent** B cells awaiting antigen encounter. - **Secondary follicles**:  Develop after antigen stimulation and contain **germinal centers** where B cells proliferate and differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells (eg, through isotype/immunoglobulin class switching) and memory B cells. - **Subcapsular sinus**:  Filters incoming lymph from afferent vessels and contains specialized macrophages that capture and present antigens to lymphocytes. ## Paracortex The paracortex is located between the cortex and medulla and primarily houses **T lymphocytes** and dendritic cells.  It contains high endothelial venules (HEVs) that allow lymphocytes to enter the node from the bloodstream (ie, via extravasation).  The paracortex enlarges when there is an extreme immune response (eg, due to infection), causing lymphadenopathy.  This region is underdeveloped in DiGeorge syndrome (ie, thymic hypoplasia affecting T-cell development). ## Medulla The medulla is the innermost region, containing the following: - **Medullary cords**:  House plasma cells and lymphocytes organized into rope-like structures. - **Medullary sinuses**:  Contain reticular cells (synthesize fibers that create a supportive meshwork) and macrophages, draining filtered lymph into efferent vessels and removing remaining pathogens. # The lymphatic system ## Lymphatic fluid Lymph, a clear fluid consisting of interstitial fluid, proteins, lipids, lymphocytes, and other immune cells that have been collected from tissues throughout the body, enters the node via multiple afferent lymphatic vessels.  Within the node, lymph is filtered as it passes through the cortex and medulla, removing pathogens and debris.  The cleansed lymph then exits the node via 1 or more efferent lymphatic vessels at the hilum ((Figure 2)).  From there, it continues through the lymphatic system before eventually draining into the venous circulation. ## Lymphatic vessels Lymphatic fluid flows through a complex network of lymphatic vessels.  Fluid from the right upper extremity, right side of the head, portions of the heart and lungs, and the right thorax drains into the **right lymphatic duct**.  The right lymphatic duct empties into the venous circulation at the junction of the right internal jugular vein and the right subclavian vein, forming the right brachiocephalic vein. In contrast, the **thoracic duct** drains lymphatic fluid from the remainder of the body, including both lower extremities, the abdomen, the left thorax, the left upper limb, and the left side of the head and neck.  The thoracic duct originates from the **cisterna chyli** in the abdomen and ascends through the thorax to empty into the venous circulation at the junction of the left internal jugular vein and the left subclavian vein, forming the left brachiocephalic vein.  The left and right brachiocephalic veins merge to form the superior vena cava, which then drains directly into the right atrium of the heart ((Figure 3)). ## Lymph node anatomy Lymph node anatomy for various structures is illustrated in the following figures:  head and neck ((Figure 4)), axillary region ((Figure 5)), lower extremities ((Figure 6)), large intestine ((Figure 7)), anorectal region ((Figure 8)), male genitalia ((Figure 9)), and female reproductive organs ((Figure 10)). # Clinical relevance Changes in lymph node characteristics provide crucial diagnostic information across multiple disciplines: - **Lymphadenopathy**:  Enlarged or tender lymph nodes frequently indicate localized infection, inflammation, or heightened immune activity in the drainage area.  The pattern of lymph node involvement may help clinicians identify the source of infection or disease.  Physical examination of lymph nodes (eg, evaluating size, consistency, tenderness, and mobility) offers valuable clinical insights.  Nodes that are hard, fixed, or painless raise concern for malignancy, whereas tender, mobile nodes typically suggest inflammatory processes. - **Regional patterns**:  The location of affected nodes corresponds to their drainage territories: - Cervical lymphadenopathy may indicate head and neck infections or malignancies. - Axillary nodes reflect upper extremity or breast pathology. - Inguinal lymphadenopathy suggests lower extremity or genitourinary conditions. - **Systemic disease markers**:  Persistent, generalized lymphadenopathy (affecting multiple nodal regions) may signal systemic conditions, including: - Autoimmune disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus). - Hematologic malignancies (lymphomas, leukemias). - Infectious diseases (HIV, tuberculosis, mononucleosis). - Metastatic cancer. - **Biopsy importance**:  Lymph node biopsy represents a critical diagnostic procedure when malignancy is suspected, providing definitive tissue diagnosis and staging information.  Fine-needle aspiration or excisional biopsy may be performed depending on the clinical context.  The **sentinel lymph node** (first node receiving drainage from a tumor site) is often evaluated to determine whether cancer has spread beyond the primary site, guiding treatment decisions, particularly in breast cancer and melanoma.  This minimizes unnecessary extensive lymph node dissection and associated complications. - Benign, reversible enlargment due to antigenic stimulus is called reactive hyperplasia.  It is classified as follicular hyperplasia (follicles increase in size and number), sinus hyperplasia (sinuses enlarge and fill with histiocytes), and diffuse hyperplasia (nodal architecture diffusely effaced by sheets of lymphocytes). - Evaluation for monoclonality of the lymphocyte population is important when lymphoma is suspected.  The clonality of a T-cell population is assessed by molecular methods (eg, PCR) that examine the rearrangement of T-cell receptor (TCR) genes.  If a single allele for the V region of the TCR predominates in a lymphocytic population, monoclonal proliferation is suspected.  Similarly, monoclonal rearrangement of the genes for immunoglobulin variable regions is suggestive of a B-cell lymphoma.  # Summary Lymph nodes are organized into cortical B-cell zones, paracortical T-cell regions, and medullary cords/sinuses.  They filter harmful substances, detect threats, and activate specific immune responses through coordinated lymphocyte interactions.  Their streamlined structure ensures efficient immune surveillance while helping to maintain fluid balance. ​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​
