articles.title: Lumbosacral Plexus
articles.markdown: # Lumbosacral Plexus # Introduction The lumbosacral plexus is a network of nerves arising from the ventral rami of spinal segments L1 through S4 that provides motor and sensory innervation to the lower extremity and pelvis.  Injuries to these nerves, caused by trauma, compression, surgery, or childbirth, produce characteristic motor and sensory deficits that allow for localization. # Organization of the plexus The lumbosacral plexus is divided into 2 parts: - **Lumbar plexus (L1-L4)**:  The lumbar plexus lies within the psoas major muscle and gives rise to the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, and obturator nerves. - **Sacral plexus (L4-S4)**:  The sacral plexus lies on the anterior surface of the piriformis muscle and gives rise to the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, sciatic, tibial, common peroneal (fibular), and pudendal nerves. Understanding the motor and sensory innervation of each terminal nerve is clinically important because these nerves are the primary sites of injury ((Figure 1)). # Major nerves of the lumbar plexus ## Iliohypogastric nerve (L1) - **Course**:  Arises primarily from the L1 nerve root, emerges from the lateral border of the upper psoas major muscle, and passes behind the kidney anterior to the quadratus lumborum. - **Motor**:  Innervates the transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles, which compress the abdominal wall and stabilize the trunk. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the suprapubic region and gluteal skin ((Figure 2)). - **Injury**:  Frequently damaged during abdominal surgeries such as appendectomy or cesarean delivery ((Figure 3)).  Findings include weakness of abdominal wall stabilization (and predisposition to herniation) and burning pain or sensory loss in the suprapubic and lateral gluteal regions. ## Ilioinguinal nerve (L1) - **Course**:  Runs inferior to the iliohypogastric nerve along the iliac crest, enters the inguinal canal, and exits through the superficial inguinal ring. - **Motor**:  Partially innervates the transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles, contributing to abdominal wall compression and trunk stabilization. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the labia majora (or anterior scrotum), mons pubis (or base of penis), and medial thigh. - **Injury**:  Often damaged during inguinal hernia repair or laparoscopic pelvic surgery.  Findings include pain or numbness in the medial thigh and genital region, sometimes with abdominal wall weakness. ## Genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2) - **Course**:  Pierces the psoas major muscle, then divides into the genital branch (traveling through the inguinal canal) and the femoral branch (passing beneath the inguinal ligament). - **Motor**:  The genital branch innervates the cremaster muscle, which elevates the testis. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the anterior scrotum or labia majora (genital branch) and to the upper anterior thigh (femoral branch). - **Injury**:  May be damaged during retroperitoneal surgery.  Findings include loss of the cremasteric reflex in males and sensory deficits in the genital region (eg, scrotum or labia majora) and upper thigh. ## Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2-L3) - **Course**:  Crosses the iliacus muscle and passes under the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine, a common entrapment site. - **Motor**:  None. - **Sensory**:  Supplies the skin of the lateral thigh. - **Injury**:  Causes meralgia paresthetica, which is a compression mononeuropathy of the nerve at the inguinal ligament, typically from tight clothing or injury during surgery (eg, hip arthroplasty).  Those with obesity, increased lumbar lordosis (eg, pregnancy), or diabetes mellitus are at increased risk ((Figure 4)).  Symptoms include burning pain, paresthesia, and numbness of the lateral thigh; strength is usually normal.  Hip extension often worsens the symptoms (possibly by compressing the nerve). ## Femoral nerve (L2-L4) - **Course**:  Descends through the psoas major, emerges from the lateral border (between the psoas and iliacus muscles), and passes under the inguinal ligament into the femoral triangle, within which lie (lateral to medial) the femoral nerve, the femoral artery, the femoral vein, and deep inguinal nodes ((Figure 5)).  (Right below the inguinal ligament—in the inguinal crease—at the lateral border of the femoral artery is the optimal site for a femoral nerve block.) - **Motor**:  Innervates the quadriceps femoris muscle for knee extension and the sartorius and iliopsoas muscles for hip and knee flexion. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg via the saphenous nerve ((Figure 6)). - **Injury**:  May result from trauma (eg, pelvic fracture), compression from a hematoma or abscess, or injury during surgery or childbirth ((Figure 7)).  Findings include weak hip flexion, impaired knee extension, loss of the patellar reflex, and sensory loss over the anterior thigh and medial leg. ## Obturator nerve (L2-L4) - **Course**:  Arises from the lumbar plexus and carries fibers from the L2-L4 spinal segments.  It descends posteromedially to the iliopsoas muscle and courses along the lateral aspect of the lesser pelvis before descending through the obturator canal ((Figure 8)).  The obturator nerve is the only major nerve that exits the pelvis through this canal. - **Motor**:  Supplies the hip adductors (adductor longus, brevis, magnus, and gracilis muscles), which bring the thigh toward the midline, and the obturator externus, which externally rotates the thigh. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the medial thigh ((Figure 9)). - **Injury**:  Occurs with compression from pelvic trauma, surgery (eg, retroperitoneal pelvic lymph node dissection), or tumors (eg, bladder cancer).  Findings include weak hip adduction, instability when walking, and numbness in the medial thigh. # Major nerves of the sacral plexus ## Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) - **Course**:  Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen *above* the piriformis. - **Motor**:  Innervates the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fascia lata, which abduct and medially rotate the thigh and stabilize the pelvis during walking. - **Sensory**:  None. - **Injury**:  May follow pelvic trauma, hip surgery, or buttocks injections, especially in the superomedial quadrant.  Findings include weakness of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles, which cause the pelvis to sag toward the unaffected (contralateral) side when the patient stands on the affected leg (positive **Trendelenburg sign**).  When walking, patients lean toward the affected (ipsilateral) side to compensate for the hip drop (gluteus medius lurch) ((Figure 10)). ## Inferior gluteal nerve (L5-S2) - **Course**:  Exits pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen *below* the piriformis muscle. - **Motor**:  Innervates the gluteus maximus muscle, which extends and laterally rotates the thigh, especially during rising from a seated position or climbing stairs. - **Sensory**:  None. - **Injury**:  May occur with hip surgery, injections, or posterior dislocations.  Findings include difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, or running, due to weakness in hip extension. ## Sciatic nerve (L4-S3) - **Course**:  Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle, runs posterior to the hip joint, and runs down the posterior thigh.  The sciatic nerve branches into the common fibular (peroneal) nerve and the tibial nerve posteriorly in the thigh proximal to the popliteal fossa ((Figure 11)). - **Motor**:  Innervates the hamstrings, which extend the hip and flex the knee.  It then divides into the tibial and common peroneal branches for leg and foot movements. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the posterior thigh and, via its branches, nearly the entire leg and foot (except the medial aspect, which is innervated by the saphenous nerve) ((Figure 12)). - **Injury**:  Can be injured via posterior hip dislocation ((Figure 13)), posterior hip surgery, or penetrating trauma.  Findings include weak hip extension, weak knee flexion, weakness of ankle dorsiflexion (foot drop from peroneal involvement), and widespread sensory loss below the knee.  The Achilles reflex may be affected if the tibial division is compromised. ## Tibial nerve (L4-S3, branch of sciatic nerve) - **Course**:  Runs through the popliteal fossa down the posterior leg and passes behind the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel. - **Motor**:  Innervates the posterior leg muscles (gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus), enabling plantar flexion, inversion, and toe flexion.  It also innervates the intrinsic plantar muscles. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the sole ((Figure 14)). - **Injury**:  Can be damaged by knee trauma or entrapment in the tarsal tunnel due to overuse (eg, tarsal tunnel syndrome), such as in running ((Figure 15)).  Findings include inability to stand on tiptoes, loss of plantarflexion, impaired toe flexion, and sensory loss on the sole.  The **Achilles reflex** (S1–S2) is diminished or absent. - Tarsal tunnel syndrome often presents with burning, neuropathic pain, numbness, and muscle cramps in the nerve distribution, primarily the posteromedial ankle, heel, sole, and toes.  The pain, worsened with weight bearing and relieved by rest, is reproduced by percussing the nerve in the posterior medial malleolar area (Tinel sign) or by dorsiflexion-eversion and plantar flexion–inversion of the ankle, which stress and compress the nerve. ## Common fibular (peroneal) nerve (L4-S2, branch of sciatic nerve) - **Course**:  Winds laterally around the fibular head and neck, where it is superficial and prone to compression or trauma, and divides into the superficial and deep peroneal nerves ((Figure 16)). - **Superficial peroneal nerve** - **Motor**:  Innervates muscles in the lateral compartment of the leg (fibularis longus and brevis), responsible primarily for foot eversion. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the anterolateral leg and most of the dorsum of the foot ((Figure 17)). - **Injury** (branch-specific):  Leads to weak foot eversion and sensory loss over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, both via entrapment or trauma. - **Deep peroneal nerve** - **Motor**:  Innervates the anterior compartment of the leg (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus), which dorsiflexes the ankle and extends the toes. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the web space between the first and second toes ((Figure 18)). - **Injury** (branch-specific):  Causes foot drop due to loss of dorsiflexion and toe extension, often resulting in a steppage gait, which is characterized by excessive hip and knee flexion to clear the toes.  Sensory loss is limited to the first web space. - **Injury (common trunk)**:  Compresses the nerve at the fibular neck from leg crossing, external pressure due to prolonged immobility (eg, hospitalization, surgery, casting), or fibular neck fracture, all of which are common ((Figure 19)).  Findings include foot drop from loss of dorsiflexion, impaired foot eversion, and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.  If the lesion is specific to a branch, deficits may be restricted. ## Pudendal nerve (S2-S4) - **Course**:  Originates from the ventral rami of S2-S4 and passes between the piriformis and the coccygeus muscles as it exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.  It then reenters through the lesser sciatic foramen near the ischial spine before dividing into its terminal branches. - **Motor**:  Innervates the external urethral and anal sphincters, which maintain continence. - **Sensory**:  Provides sensation to the perineum. - **Injury**:  Can be injured during a prolonged second stage of labor or forceps-assisted delivery because of its curved course around the ischial spine ((Figure 20)).  It can also be injured during pelvic surgery.  Findings include urinary and fecal incontinence and sensory loss in the perineal region, which is often worse with sitting.  The **anal wink reflex** (S2-S4) may be absent. # Reflexes by spinal level - **Cremasteric reflex** (L1-L2, genitofemoral nerve):  Stroking the inner thigh causes ipsilateral testicular elevation; it is absent in genitofemoral injury. - **Patellar reflex** (L2-L4, femoral nerve):  Tapping the patellar tendon produces knee extension; it is absent in femoral nerve injury. - **Achilles reflex** (S1-S2, tibial nerve):  Tapping the Achilles tendon produces plantarflexion; it is absent in tibial or sciatic injury. - **Anal wink reflex** (S2-S4, pudendal nerve):  Stroking the perianal region causes contraction of the external anal sphincter; it is absent in pudendal injury. # Summary Injuries to the lumbosacral plexus are best localized by analyzing the motor and sensory territories of individual nerves within the lumbar and sacral divisions.  Each nerve's muscle actions clarify the functional deficits expected after injury, whereas reflexes linked to specific spinal levels and nerves provide additional clinical clues for localization.​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌

# Histology: Epithelial Tissue # Introduction Epithelial tissues cover external surfaces, line internal spaces, and form the secretory units of glands.  Each epithelial cell has an apical surface facing a lumen or an external environment and a basal surface attached to underlying connective tissue.  This polarity facilitates the function of epithelial tissues as selective barriers, exchange interfaces, and secretion or absorption structures. # Polarity Cell polarity refers to a functional asymmetry that organizes the cell membrane into distinct regions specialized for different tasks.  Epithelial cells have apical-basal (or luminal-basal) polarity, which distinguishes the surface facing the lumen from the surface attached to an underlying structure called the basement membrane.  The mechanical cohesion and barrier integrity of epithelial cells rely on junctional structures that link neighboring cells and anchor them to the basement membrane. ## Apical membrane The apical membrane (ie, facing the lumen or external environment) of epithelial cells often contains specialized structures that enhance absorption or transport.  These include the following: - **Microvilli** are actin-based membrane projections that increase apical surface area.  They are prominent in absorptive epithelia, such as the intestinal mucosa (eg, intestinal brush border ((Figure 1))) and renal proximal tubule. - **Cilia** ((Figure 2)) are microtubule-based projections that produce coordinated beating motions.  Motile cilia contain a characteristic 9 + 2 microtubule arrangement (circular array of 9 microtubule doublets surrounding 2 central microtubules) and move fluid or particles across epithelial surfaces, as in the respiratory tract and uterine tubes. - **Stereocilia** are long, actin-based projections that resemble microvilli but are much longer.  They are found in the epididymis and function primarily in absorption. ## Basolateral membrane The basolateral membrane contains transporters, receptors, and adhesion molecules that interact with underlying tissues.  This polarity enables directional transport of molecules. ## Basement membrane The basement membrane is a thin extracellular layer that separates epithelium from underlying connective tissue.  Its components include: - **Basal lamina**:  Produced by epithelial cells and composed primarily of type IV collagen, laminin, and proteoglycans. - **Reticular lamina**:  Derived from underlying connective tissue and composed mainly of type III collagen. These anchor epithelial cells and regulate cell polarity and differentiation.  The basement membrane provides structural support and can serve for biochemical signaling or as a filtration barrier in specialized tissues (eg, glomerulus) ((Figure 3)). ## Junctional structures Key junctional structures include ((Figure 4)): - Tight junctions form a continuous apical seal, creating an impermeable barrier to diffusion. - Adherens junctions form a belt just beneath tight junctions, providing a dynamic (ie, calcium-dependent) but strong link between cells. - Desmosomes form discrete spot-like junctions that anchor the lateral surfaces of adjacent cells together, providing tensile strength. - Hemidesmosomes (fixed) and focal adhesion complexes (transient) attach the basal cell surface to the basement membrane. - Gap junctions enable direct cytoplasmic exchange for synchronized electrical and metabolic activity (eg, heart contraction). They are described in more detail in a separate article. # Classification: Cell layers and shapes Epithelia are classified based on the number of layers and the shape of the epithelial cells ((Figure 5)). ## Cell layers - **Simple epithelium**:  Composed of a single cell layer.  Because all cells contact the basement membrane, this organization is optimized for absorption, secretion, and exchange - **Stratified epithelium**:  Composed of multiple layers.  The different layers provide mechanical protection in areas exposed to friction or stress. ## Cell shape This organization is based on the shape of the **superficial layer** of cells: - **Squamous**:  Flattened cells with thin cytoplasm that facilitates diffusion. - **Cuboidal**:  Cells with approximately equal height and width, typically involved in secretion or absorption. - **Columnar**:  Tall cells specialized for absorption, secretion, or mucus production. The combination of these categories based on the number of layers and shape leads to the classic epithelial categories: - Simple squamous epithelium in the alveoli, optimized for gas exchange and diffusion. - Simple columnar epithelium in the intestine, optimized for secretion or absorption. - Stratified squamous epithelium in the epidermis or vagina ((Figure 6)), optimized for mechanical protection. An additional characteristic could describe whether the superficial layer has keratin or not. ## Special classifications - **Pseudostratified epithelium** appears multilayered; however, all cells contact the basement membrane, but not all reach the surface.  This organization is often associated with specialized apical structures such as cilia. - **Transitional epithelium**, or urothelium, is a stratified epithelium that can distend and is found in the lower urinary tract. ## Transformation (metaplasia) Certain epithelial cells can convert from one type to another, typically as an adaptive mechanism in response to a stimulus or stress.  Most commonly, columnar-to-squamous epithelium can occur in normal pseudostratified columnar respiratory epithelium in response to smoking ((Figure 7)) or in cervical epithelium in response to infection.  Squamous-to-columnar metaplasia can occur in Barrett esophagus, in which chronic reflux esophagitis can trigger the replacement of normal squamous epithelium in the distal esophagus with metaplastic columnar epithelium ((Figure 8)). ## Special naming conventions The epithelial lining of blood and lymph vessels is called **endothelium** ((Figure 9)), that of heart ventricles and atria is called **endocardium**, and that covering closed body cavities (abdominal, pericardial, pleural) is called **mesothelium**. # Epithelial renewal Epithelial tissues undergo continuous renewal because surface cells are exposed to mechanical and environmental stress.  Proliferation occurs in a basal population of stem or progenitor cells attached to the basement membrane.  Older cells migrate toward the surface and eventually undergo apoptosis or are shed. The rate of renewal varies widely.  Intestinal epithelium turns over within days, whereas epidermal keratinocytes in the skin differentiate and reach the surface over several weeks.  This renewal capacity allows epithelial tissues to maintain barrier function despite constant environmental stress (trauma, injury). # Epithelial glands Epithelia also form **glands**, structures specialized for secretion, by invaginating into underlying connective tissue and forming secretory units that retain epithelial characteristics. Two major categories are recognized:  exocrine and endocrine. ## Exocrine glands Exocrine glands ((Figure 10)) secrete products onto epithelial surfaces through ducts (eg, sweat glands, salivary glands).  They are classified as mucous (mucus secretions) or serous (watery, protein-rich secretions), with 3 mechanisms of secretion: merocrine, apocrine, and holocrine ((Table 1)). Exocrine glands can be unicellular (eg, goblet cells in the intestine) or multicellular and simple (unbranched duct) or compound (branched duct).  Depending on the shape of the secretory portion, the gland can be tubular (shaped like a tube), alveolar/acinar (shaped like a flask), or tubuloalveolar (shaped like a sac). ## Endocrine glands Endocrine glands do not have ducts and release hormones directly into the bloodstream, with the target receptor on distant cells ((Figure 11)). Secretory cells often show specialized cytologic features reflecting their products.  For example, protein-secreting cells contain abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, whereas corticosteroid-secreting cells have extensive smooth endoplasmic reticulum and lipid droplets. # Summary Epithelial tissues cover external surfaces, line internal spaces, and form glands.  Their structure is defined by apical-basal polarity, which organizes the membrane into regions facing the lumen and the underlying connective tissue.  Junctional complexes maintain cohesion and barrier integrity, whereas the basement membrane anchors epithelial cells and provides structural support and signaling.  Epithelia are classified by cell layering and the shape of superficial cells, producing types adapted for diffusion, absorption, secretion, or protection.  Through invagination into connective tissue, epithelial cells also form exocrine and endocrine glands specialized for secretion.  Continuous renewal from basal progenitor cells maintains epithelial integrity despite ongoing environmental stress, allowing epithelial tissues to function as barriers, regulate permeability, absorb nutrients and fluids, secrete substances, and transport material across surfaces. ​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌

# Gastrointestinal Anatomy And Histology III: Large Intestine, Rectum/Anus

# Introduction

The gastrointestinal (GI) tract, also known as the alimentary canal, is a continuous tube extending from the mouth to the anus.  It is approximately 9 m long and includes the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), large intestine (cecum to rectum), and anal canal.  Its primary functions are digestion, absorption, secretion, and excretion.  Structurally, it consists of specialized regions with distinct anatomic and histologic adaptations suited to their roles ((Figure 1)).  This article focuses on the large intestine, rectum, and anal canal, which are responsible for fluid absorption, fecal storage, and controlled elimination.

# Overview of embryology and core histologic organization

The GI tract develops from an endoderm-derived primitive gut tube that is partitioned into foregut, midgut, and hindgut, establishing the pattern of vascular supply, innervation, and lymphatic drainage ((Figure 2)).  The hindgut extends from the distal transverse colon to the upper anal canal.  Hindgut derivatives are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), receive parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4), and sympathetic input via the inferior mesenteric plexus.  The distal anal canal arises from the ectoderm and is separated from the endoderm-derived hindgut by the pectinate line, marking abrupt transitions in vascular supply, innervation, and lymphatic drainage.

The gastrointestinal wall has a common organization consisting of mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and an outer serosa or adventitia.

-   The mucosa is composed of epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae.  The epithelium is simple columnar throughout the colon and rectum, specialized for water and electrolyte absorption and mucus secretion, and transitions to stratified squamous epithelium in the distal anal canal for protection against mechanical stress.  The lamina propria contains vascular, glandular, and immune elements, and the muscularis mucosae facilitates local mucosal movement.
-   The submucosa consists of dense connective tissue containing larger blood vessels, lymphatics, and glands and houses the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, which regulates mucosal secretion, local blood flow, and fluid transport.
-   The muscularis externa, composed of inner circular and outer longitudinal layers, drives segmentation and peristalsis under control of the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus; the longitudinal layer is organized into teniae coli in the colon and becomes continuous in the rectum. 
-   The outer layer varies by location.  Intraperitoneal segments are covered by serosa (visceral peritoneum), which provides a smooth, lubricated surface that facilitates movement.  Retroperitoneal portions of the colon and the distal rectum and anal canal are covered by adventitia, which lacks mesothelium and instead anchors these structures to surrounding tissues.

# Large intestine

## Gross anatomy

The large intestine includes the cecum, colon, rectum, and anal canal.  It is shorter than the small intestine but has a larger lumen diameter, which is greatest at the cecum (approximately 9 cm).  The proximal portions of the large intestine (from the cecum to the transverse colon) function primarily to absorb water, electrolytes, and vitamins produced by intestinal bacteria, whereas the distal portions (descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and anal canal) function mainly in the storage and elimination of fecal material.

Grossly, the colon can be distinguished from the small intestine by the presence of haustra, teniae coli, and epiploic appendices.  Haustra are sacculations of the colonic wall that occur along its length and result from contraction of the teniae coli, in contrast to the circular folds of the small intestine ((Figure 3)).  The teniae coli are 3 longitudinal bands of smooth muscle that begin at the base of the appendix and run along the length of the colon, converging at the rectosigmoid junction, where they spread to form the continuous longitudinal muscle layer of the rectum.  Epiploic appendices are fat-filled pouches of peritoneum that project from the external surface of the colon and are most prominent along the transverse and sigmoid colon.

## Anatomic relationships

-   **Cecum**:  Lies in the right lower quadrant.  It is intraperitoneal and mobile and receives contents from the small intestine through the ileocecal valve.  The appendix arises from the posteromedial aspect of the cecum.
-   **Ascending colon**:  Lies retroperitoneal and runs superiorly along the right side of the abdomen from the cecum to the hepatic (right colic) flexure, where it turns medially to become the transverse colon.  It lies anterior to the right kidney and inferior to the right lobe of the liver.
-   **Transverse colon**:  Extends across the upper abdomen from the hepatic flexure on the right to the splenic (left colic) flexure on the left and is supported near its left end by the phrenicocolic ligament, which attaches to the diaphragm.  It lies inferior to the stomach, liver, and gallbladder; posterior to the greater omentum; and anterior to the pancreas, duodenum, and portions of the jejunum and ileum.  The transverse colon is intraperitoneal and suspended by the transverse mesocolon, making it relatively mobile compared with the ascending and descending colon.
-   **Descending colon**:  Lies retroperitoneal and descends along the left side of the abdomen from the splenic flexure to approximately the level of the **iliac crest**, where it continues as the sigmoid colon.  It lies anterior to the left kidney and the lateral abdominal wall.
-   **Sigmoid colon**:  Located intraperitoneally and suspended by the sigmoid mesocolon.  It lies within the pelvis and courses from the left lower quadrant toward the midline, forming an S-shaped curve as it travels anterior to the sacrum before continuing as the rectum.

## Blood, lymphatic, and nerve supply

-   **Arterial supply**:  Consists of branches of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) for the proximal large intestine (a derivative of the midgut) and branches of the IMA for the distal colon beyond the splenic flexure (a hindgut derivative).  These arterial systems communicate through the marginal artery (of Drummond), a continuous arterial channel that runs along the inner border of the colon and provides collateral circulation.
    -   Cecum:  Supplied primarily by the ileocolic artery, a branch of the SMA.
    -   Ascending colon:  Supplied by the ileocolic and right colic arteries, branches of the SMA.
    -   Transverse colon:  Supplied mainly by the middle colic artery (from the SMA), with contribution near the splenic flexure from the left colic artery (from the IMA).
    -   Descending colon:  Supplied by the left colic artery, a branch of the IMA.
    -   Sigmoid colon:  Supplied by the sigmoid arteries, branches of the IMA.

Two clinically important **watershed areas** exist in the large intestine, where arterial territories meet, and collateral circulation is relatively limited: **at the splenic flexure** (between the middle colic branch of the SMA and the left colic branch of the IMA) and **at the rectosigmoid junction** (between the last sigmoid arterial branch and the superior rectal artery).  Because these regions lie at the borders of arterial supply, they are **particularly vulnerable to ischemia during systemic hypotension or shock**, when reduced perfusion pressure can lead to **ischemic colitis**, most commonly affecting the splenic flexure.

-   **Venous drainage** ((Figure 4)):  Generally parallels the arterial supply.  Midgut derivatives (cecum, ascending colon, and proximal transverse colon) drain into the superior mesenteric vein (SMV).  Hindgut derivatives (distal transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum) drain into the inferior mesenteric vein, which typically empties into the splenic vein.  The splenic vein and SMV then unite to form the portal vein, which carries nutrient-rich blood to the liver ((Figure 5)).  The inferior portion of the anal canal drains via the middle and inferior rectal veins into the internal iliac venous system, representing a connection between the portal and systemic venous circulations ((Figure 6)).
-   **Lymphatic drainage**:  Generally follows the course of the colonic arteries.  Lymph from the cecum, ascending colon, and proximal transverse colon drains into the ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic lymph nodes, which ultimately empty into the superior mesenteric lymph nodes.  Lymph from the distal transverse colon, descending colon, and sigmoid colon drains into the left colic and sigmoid lymph nodes, which then drain into the inferior mesenteric lymph nodes.  From these nodes, lymph passes to the intestinal lymphatic trunks and cisterna chyli, eventually entering the thoracic duct.
-   **Nerve supply**:  Provided by both parasympathetic and sympathetic components of the autonomic nervous system.  Parasympathetic innervation to the proximal large intestine (midgut derivatives) is supplied by the vagus nerve, whereas the distal large intestine (hindgut derivatives) receives parasympathetic input from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4), which stimulate colonic motility and secretion.  Sympathetic innervation arises from lumbar splanchnic nerves that synapse in the inferior mesenteric ganglion and travel through the inferior mesenteric plexus, generally inhibiting intestinal motility and secretion and promoting vasoconstriction.  These autonomic fibers interact with the enteric nervous system, which coordinates local motility and digestive activity within the colon.

## Microscopic anatomy

-   **Mucosa**
    -   Most of the large intestine is lined by simple columnar epithelium without villi.
    -   **Intestinal glands** ((Figure 7)) (ie, colonic crypts) are straight tubular glands that extend into the mucosa and contain stem cells at their bases for epithelial renewal and numerous mucus-producing goblet cells, which increase in abundance in the distal colon and rectum to facilitate lubrication of fecal material.
-   **Submucosa**:  Contains connective tissue, vessels, nerves, and lymphoid tissue.  Lymphoid aggregates may extend from the lamina propria into the submucosa and are particularly dense in the appendix, reflecting its role in immune surveillance.
-   **Muscularis externa**:  Consists of 2 layers.  The inner circular layer is continuous and circumferential throughout the large intestine.  This layer contracts to narrow the lumen, promotes segmentation (mixing), and contributes to peristalsis by pushing contents forward when contraction occurs behind a bolus.  The outer longitudinal layer exists from the cecum to the rectum: It is condensed into 3 bands called the teniae coli, which contribute to the formation of haustra.  This layer contracts to shorten the intestinal segment, which helps pull the bowel over the luminal contents and assists in propelling material distally during peristalsis.
-   **Serosa/adventitia**:  Present around different organs.  Serosa covers intraperitoneal portions ((Figure 8)), whereas adventitia is present in retroperitoneal segments, anchoring the colon to surrounding structures.

# Rectum

The rectum begins at the rectosigmoid junction and extends inferiorly to the anal canal.  The upper portion of the rectum is covered by the peritoneum anteriorly and laterally.  Inferiorly, the peritoneum reflects anteriorly to form the rectovesical pouch in males (with the rectum lying posterior to the bladder and prostate) and the rectouterine pouch in females (with the rectum lying posterior to the uterus and vagina).  The rectum lies anterior to the sacrum and coccyx and is supported inferiorly by the pelvic floor musculature, which helps maintain continence and supports the pelvic viscera.

## Blood, lymphatic, and nerve supply

-   **Arterial supply**:  Receives blood from 3 primary arteries.  The superior rectal artery, a continuation of the IMA, supplies the proximal rectum.  The middle rectal arteries, branches of the internal iliac arteries, supply the midrectum and contribute to anastomoses with the superior rectal artery.  The inferior rectal arteries, branches of the internal pudendal arteries (from the internal iliac), supply the distal rectum and anal canal.  These vessels form an extensive anastomotic network within the rectal wall.
-   **Venous drainage**:  Parallels the arterial supply and forms an important connection between the portal and systemic venous systems.  The superior rectal vein drains the upper rectum into the inferior mesenteric vein, which then drains into the splenic and portal veins.  The middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac vein, which ultimately empties into the inferior vena cava.  This dual drainage creates a portosystemic (portocaval) anastomosis in the rectum.
-   **Lymphatic drainage**:  Follows the arterial supply.  The upper rectum drains to the inferior mesenteric lymph nodes, whereas the middle and lower rectum drain to the internal iliac lymph nodes.
-   **Innervation**:  Provided by autonomic fibers through the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus.  Parasympathetic innervation arises from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) and stimulates rectal motility and relaxation of the internal anal sphincter during defecation.  Sympathetic innervation is supplied by fibers from the lumbar splanchnic nerves via the superior hypogastric and inferior hypogastric plexuses, which generally inhibit rectal motility and promote contraction of the internal anal sphincter.  These autonomic inputs coordinate with the enteric nervous system to regulate rectal function.

## Microscopic anatomy

-   **Mucosa**:  Lined by simple columnar epithelium, similar to the colon, and contains numerous goblet cells that secrete mucus to lubricate fecal material and facilitate its passage.  The mucosa forms straight tubular glands (rectal crypts) that extend into the lamina propria and contain stem cells for epithelial renewal.
-   **Submucosa**:  Consists of dense connective tissue containing blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves, including the Meissner (submucosal) plexus, which helps regulate mucosal secretion and local blood flow.  This layer also contains elastic fibers that allow the rectum to distend as fecal material accumulates.
-   **Muscularis externa**:  Has the typical inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of smooth muscle.  In contrast to the colon, the teniae coli spread out and fuse to form a continuous longitudinal layer in the rectum.  In addition, the inner circular layer forms three transverse folds called the valves of Houston, which project into the lumen and help support the weight of fecal material within the rectum.  Coordinated contractions of these layers generate peristaltic movements that propel fecal material toward the anal canal during defecation.
-   **Serosa/adventitia**:  Represent the outer covering of the rectum, which varies along its length.  The upper portion is partially covered by serosa (visceral peritoneum), whereas the middle and lower portions are surrounded by adventitia, which anchors the rectum to surrounding pelvic structures.

# Anal canal and anus

The anal canal is extraperitoneal and joins the rectum at an angle, which helps maintain continence, and is approximately 3-4 cm long.  It extends from the anorectal junction to the anal verge and travels inferiorly and posteriorly between the ischioanal fossae on either side.  The canal is surrounded by the internal anal sphincter, a thickening of the inner circular smooth muscle layer that maintains involuntary tone, and the external anal sphincter, composed of skeletal muscle that provides voluntary control of defecation.  The pectinate (dentate) line divides the anal canal into superior and inferior portions with distinct embryologic origins, vascular supply, innervation, and lymphatic drainage.

## Blood, lymphatic, and nerve supply

-   **Arterial supply** ((Figure 9)):  Receives blood from 3 primary sources.  The superior rectal artery, a continuation of the IMA, supplies the portion of the canal above the pectinate line.  The middle rectal arteries, branches of the internal iliac arteries, provide additional supply to the region.  The inferior rectal arteries, branches of the internal pudendal arteries (from the internal iliac), supply the portion of the anal canal below the pectinate line.  These arteries form an anastomotic network within the anal canal.
-   **Venous drainage**:  Reflects the division at the pectinate line and forms an important portosystemic (portocaval) anastomosis.  The superior rectal vein drains the region above the pectinate line into the inferior mesenteric vein and portal system.  The middle and inferior rectal veins drain the region below the pectinate line into the internal iliac vein and systemic circulation.
-   **Lymphatic drainage**:  Also differs above and below the pectinate line.  The superior portion of the anal canal drains to the internal iliac lymph nodes, whereas the inferior portion drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, reflecting its distinct embryologic origin.
-   **Innervation**:  Differs on either side of the pectinate line.  The upper anal canal receives visceral autonomic innervation from the inferior hypogastric plexus, including parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) and sympathetic fibers from the lumbar splanchnic nerves; this region is relatively insensitive to pain, temperature, and touch.  The lower anal canal receives somatic sensory and motor innervation from the inferior rectal nerves, branches of the pudendal nerve, making this region highly sensitive to pain, temperature, and touch and allowing voluntary control of the external anal sphincter.

## Microscopic anatomy

-   **Mucosa**:  Transitions epithelial type along its length.  Above the dentate line, the mucosa is lined by simple columnar epithelium similar to that of the rectum and contains intestinal glands.  Below the dentate line (which represents the embryologic junction where endoderm meets ectoderm), the epithelium transitions to stratified squamous epithelium, which becomes keratinized at the anal verge as it merges with the skin.
-   **Submucosa**:  Consists of connective tissue containing blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves.  In the anal canal, it contains a rich venous plexus, which contributes to the formation of internal and external hemorrhoids when dilated.
-   **Muscularis externa**:  Differs between the internal and external anal sphincters.  The inner circular layer of the muscularis externa is thickened in the anal canal to form the internal anal sphincter ((Figure 10)).  This sphincter is composed of smooth muscle, is under involuntary autonomic control, and helps maintain continence at rest.  The external anal sphincter is separate from the bowel wall and is composed of skeletal muscle under voluntary control, allowing conscious control of defecation.
-   **Adventitia**:  The anal canal is extraperitoneal and therefore covered by adventitia rather than serosa, which anchors it to surrounding perineal structures.

# Summary

The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes and compacts intestinal contents into feces, with haustra and teniae coli supporting mixing and propulsion.  Its vascular supply reflects the transition from superior to inferior mesenteric territories, with watershed areas prone to ischemia.  The rectum stores fecal material and coordinates defecation, whereas the anal canal maintains continence through internal and external sphincters.  Together, these regions concentrate indigestible material, regulate storage, and enable controlled elimination.

​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​

articles.markdown: # Gastrointestinal Anatomy And Histology I: Oropharynx And Esophagus # Introduction The gastrointestinal (GI) tract, also known as the alimentary canal, is a continuous tube extending from the mouth to the anus.  It is approximately 9 m long and includes the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), large intestine (cecum to rectum), and anal canal.  Its primary functions are digestion, absorption, secretion, and excretion.  Structurally, it consists of specialized regions with distinct anatomic and histologic adaptations suited to their roles ((Figure 1)).  This article focuses on the upper GI tract, including the mouth, pharynx, and esophagus. # Overview of embryology and core histologic organization The oral cavity and pharynx arise largely from the pharyngeal arches and mark the proximal entry to the gastrointestinal tract.  Distally, the remainder of the GI tract develops from an endoderm-derived primitive gut tube that is partitioned into foregut, midgut, and hindgut, establishing the pattern of vascular supply, innervation, and lymphatic drainage ((Figure 2)).  The foregut extends from the oropharynx to the proximal duodenum and gives rise to the esophagus and stomach; its derivatives are supplied by branches of the celiac trunk and receive parasympathetic innervation from the vagus nerve and sympathetic input via the celiac plexus. From the esophagus distally, the GI wall shares a common histologic organization consisting of mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and an outer adventitia or serosa. - The mucosa (innermost layer) is composed of epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae.  The epithelium lines the lumen of the GI tract and functions in absorption, digestion, and secretion while also serving as a barrier to pathogens and toxins.  Most of the GI tract is lined by simple columnar epithelium, although the proximal and distal ends (eg, oropharynx, esophagus, portions of the anal canal) contain stratified squamous epithelium for protection against mechanical stress, with a transition to simple columnar epithelium at the gastroesophageal junction.  The lamina propria, a layer of loose connective tissue, contains blood vessels, glands, and immune cells, and the muscularis mucosae generates localized movements that facilitate secretion. - The submucosa consists of dense connective tissue containing larger vessels, lymphatics, and glands and houses the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, an enteric nervous system component that regulates secretion and local blood flow. - The muscularis externa, composed of inner circular and outer longitudinal layers, drives peristalsis under the control of the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, also a component of the enteric nervous system. - The outer layer varies by location.  In intraperitoneal segments, serosa (visceral peritoneum), a thin connective tissue layer covered by mesothelium, provides a smooth, lubricated surface.  In extraperitoneal segments, it is the adventitia, a connective tissue layer that lacks mesothelium and anchors the organ to surrounding structures.  Accordingly, the esophagus is predominantly covered by adventitia along its cervical and thoracic course, with only the short abdominal segment invested by serosa. # Mouth and pharynx ## Gross anatomy The oral cavity functions in ingestion, mastication, and the initial stages of digestion while also contributing to speech and respiration.  The roof of the oral cavity is formed by the hard palate anteriorly and the soft palate posteriorly.  Accessory structures include the teeth and the tongue, which is composed of 8 skeletal muscles that assist with food manipulation and swallowing.  The oral cavity is kept moist by secretions from the major salivary glands (ie, parotid, submandibular, sublingual) and numerous minor salivary glands, which begin the chemical digestion of food. Posterior to the oral cavity lies the pharynx, a muscular passage that serves as a common pathway for both food and air.  It is divided into 3 regions: nasopharynx (most superior and part of the respiratory tract), oropharynx (posterior to the oral cavity), and laryngopharynx (most inferior).  Inferiorly, the pharynx continues as the esophagus, and anteriorly it communicates with the larynx.  During swallowing, the epiglottis closes over the laryngeal inlet to prevent food from entering the airway ((Figure 3)).  The oral cavity and pharynx also contain tonsils, aggregates of lymphoid tissue that contribute to immune defense against inhaled or ingested pathogens. ## Blood, lymphatic, and nerve supply - **Arterial supply**:  Consists primarily of branches of the external carotid artery (eg, lingual, maxillary, alveolar, ascending pharyngeal, ascending and descending palatine arteries). - **Venous drainage**:  Generally follows the arterial supply and drains to the internal and external jugular veins. - **Lymphatics**:  Drain primarily to the deep cervical lymph nodes. - **Nerve supply**:  Provided by several cranial nerves, including the trigeminal nerve (CN V), facial nerve (CN VII), glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), and vagus nerve (CN X). ## Microscopic anatomy - **Oral cavity** - **Mucosa**:  Lined by stratified squamous epithelium, which is keratinized in regions subject to greater mechanical stress (eg,  hard palate, gingiva).  The mucosa of the tongue contains papillae and taste buds involved in gustation. - **Submucosa**:  Represents a connective tissue layer underlying the mucosa in some parts of the oral cavity.  It contains minor salivary glands throughout the oral cavity (except for the gingiva and anterior portion of the hard palate) with serous or mucinous acini that produce serous or mucous secretions to help lubricate the oral cavity. - **Pharynx** - **Mucosa**:  Lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium in the oropharynx and laryngopharynx and by ciliated, pseudostratified columnar (respiratory) epithelium in the nasopharynx. - **Submucosa**:  Consists of connective tissue containing blood vessels and mucous glands. - **Muscularis**:  Consists of: - Inner longitudinal layer:  Stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus, and salpingopharyngeus muscles elevate the pharynx during swallowing. - Outer circular layer:  Propels food toward the esophagus (group of constrictor muscles). - **Adventitia**:  Consists of a fibrous connective tissue layer that anchors the pharynx to surrounding structures. # Esophagus  ## Gross anatomy The esophagus is a muscular tube that is 25 cm long and transports swallowed food and liquids from the pharynx to the stomach through coordinated peristaltic contractions.  It travels through the thorax and passes through the diaphragm to connect to the stomach ((Figure 4)).  The upper esophageal sphincter (UES) is composed of skeletal muscle (an inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle called the cricopharyngeus) and is located at the junction of the laryngopharynx and esophagus.  The UES opens during the swallowing reflex to allow passage of a food bolus into the esophagus and remains closed at rest to prevent reflux of esophageal contents into the pharynx and airway.  The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is composed of smooth muscle and remains closed at rest to prevent reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus.  Peristaltic contractions of the esophageal wall propel the food bolus distally, whereas relaxation of the LES allows the bolus to enter the stomach. ## Anatomic relationships - In the cervical region and upper mediastinum, the esophagus lies posterior and slightly to the left of the trachea and anterior to the vertebral column.  Below the bifurcation of the trachea, the esophagus lies between the heart anteriorly (particularly the left atrium) and the thoracic aorta posteriorly ((Figure 5)). - The left recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove along the anterior aspect of the esophagus as it travels toward the larynx. - The thoracic duct runs posterior to the esophagus as it ascends through the posterior mediastinum. - The vagus nerves form the esophageal plexus on the surface of the esophagus; these fibers reorganize inferiorly into the anterior and posterior vagal trunks, which pass with the esophagus through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm at the T10 vertebral level. - The aortic arch and left main bronchus cross the esophagus in the superior and middle mediastinum, respectively, producing normal physiologic constrictions. ## Blood, lymphatic, and nerve supply - **Arterial supply**:  Consists of anastomoses running along the course of the esophagus and supplied by the inferior thyroid, intercostal, gastric, and inferior phrenic arteries. - **Venous drainage**:  Occurs via the azygos and hemiazygos veins for the upper esophagus and via the left gastric vein for the lower esophagus ((Figure 6)), ((Figure 7)). - **Lymphatic drainage**:  Occurs through a longitudinal network that drains to deep cervical nodes (cervical esophagus), posterior mediastinal nodes (thoracic esophagus), and left gastric nodes (abdominal esophagus). - **Nerve supply**:  Consists of the vagus nerve and the sympathetic trunk. ## Microscopic anatomy - **Mucosa**:  The mucosa mostly consists of nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium for protection against abrasion and mechanical trauma ((Figure 8)).  The **Z line** at the lower esophagus marks the transition point from the stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus to the simple columnar epithelium of the stomach. - **Submucosa**:  The submucosa contains mucous esophageal glands for lubrication. - **Muscularis externa**:  The 2 layers include an inner circular layer and an outer longitudinal layer.  The upper third of the esophagus contains striated (skeletal) muscle, the middle third contains a mixture of striated and smooth muscle, and the lower third contains smooth muscle.  Coordinated contraction of these muscle layers produces peristalsis, a wave-like series of contractions that propels the swallowed bolus from the pharynx through the esophagus and toward the stomach. - **Adventitia/serosa**:  The outermost layer is composed of adventitia in the thoracic portion of the esophagus and becomes serosa inferiorly as it progresses near the stomach. # Summary The oral cavity and pharynx initiate digestion through mastication, salivary secretion, and coordinated swallowing while protecting the airway.  These regions are lined by stratified squamous epithelium and are controlled by cranial nerves that integrate sensory input with motor function.  The esophagus then transports ingested material to the stomach via peristalsis, with upper and lower sphincters regulating entry and preventing reflux.  These structures convert ingested material into a bolus and deliver it to the stomach and intestines for chemical digestion and nutrient absorption. ​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌

# Female Reproductive System Anatomy And Histology # Introduction The female reproductive system consists of the gonads (ovaries), internal genitalia (eg, fallopian tubes, uterus), and the external genitalia (eg, vulva, clitoris).  This article focuses on the function, anatomy, and histology of each component of the female reproductive system. # Ovaries The ovaries are paired structures located posterolaterally to the uterus within the ovarian fossa on the lateral walls of the pelvis, bilaterally.  They are suspended superiorly by the mesovarium, medially by the uteroovarian ligament, and laterally by the suspensory ligament of the ovary.  The suspensory ligament of the ovary, also known as the infundibulopelvic ligament, is a fold of peritoneum that attaches the ovary to the pelvic sidewall and contains the ovarian artery, ovarian vein, lymphatics, and nerves ((Figure 1)). The 2 functions of the ovary are to produce mature oocytes for reproduction and to produce sex steroids (eg, estrogen, progesterone) for secondary sexual characteristics. ## Blood supply The ovaries are supplied blood primarily through the ovarian arteries, which originate from the abdominal aorta.  However, they also receive blood from an ascending branch of the uterine artery.  Blood is removed from the ovaries through the ovarian veins: the right ovarian vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava, whereas the left ovarian vein drains into the left renal vein ((Figure 2)). ## Nerve supply The ovaries receive autonomic innervation from the ovarian plexus, which is derived from the renal and aortic plexuses. ## Lymphatic drainage The ovaries drain lymph predominantly to the paraaortic lymph nodes, although some lymph is drained to the external and internal iliac lymph nodes ((Figure 3)). ## Histology The ovary is composed of 2 major portions, the outer cortex and the central medulla. The outermost cortex is lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells (ie, ovarian surface epithelium), which is a modified mesothelium that is continuous with the peritoneum.  Within the cortex is ovarian stroma with interspersed ovarian follicles at different developmental stages ((Figure 4)).  The mature follicle consists of an oocyte (germ cell) encircled by granulosa cells and theca cells, which support the oocyte throughout follicle development. The central medulla of the ovary is predominantly composed of blood vessels and nerves within loose connective tissue. # Fallopian tubes The fallopian tubes (oviducts) are approximately 10-12 cm long and extend bilaterally from the uterine cornua.  They are divided into 3 sections: the isthmus, ampulla, and infundibulum (which contains fimbriae).  The primary function of the fallopian tube is to capture an ovulated oocyte with the fimbriae, provide a site of fertilization, and transport the zygote to the uterus. ## Blood supply The fallopian tubes receive blood through the anastomoses of the ovarian artery with an ascending branch of the uterine artery. ## Nerve supply The fallopian tubes receive autonomic innervation via the ovarian and uterine plexuses. ## Lymphatic drainage Lymph from the fallopian tubes drains primarily to the paraaortic nodes (via ovarian vessels) and iliac lymph nodes (via the uterine vessels) ((Figure 5)). ## Histology The fallopian tube has 3 layers: the mucosa, the muscularis (composed of an inner circular layer and an outer longitudinal layer), and the serosa.  The mucosa is lined with ciliated columnar cells and secretory cells.  The zygote moves through the fallopian tube toward the uterus for implantation via peristaltic contractions of the muscularis layer and the coordinated beating of the cilia, which produces laminar flow. # Uterus The uterus is a muscular organ that consists of the fundus, the uterine body, the isthmus (site of fallopian tube insertion), and the cervix.  The uterus is covered by a sheet of peritoneum extending from the uterus and upper cervix to the pelvic sidewall, known as the broad ligament ((Figure 6)).  It is divided into 3 parts: - **Mesosalpinx**:  Descends from the fallopian tube. - **Mesovarium**:  Inferior to the mesosalpinx, covers the ovarian hilum. - **Mesometrium**:  The largest portion of the broad ligament that lies inferior to the mesovarium, lateral from the uterus to external iliac vessels, and anterior to the proximal round ligament. The primary functions of the uterus are to be the site of implantation and to support fetal development.  In addition, the innermost lining of the uterus (endometrium) undergoes monthly shedding and regeneration in the menstrual cycle under the control of fluctuating hormones (eg, estrogen, progesterone). ## Blood supply The uterus is supplied blood through the uterine arteries, which are branches of the internal iliac artery.  The ureter runs close to the uterine artery, which places the ureter at risk for iatrogenic injury during hysterectomies or pelvic surgeries (eg, ureteric obstruction, hydronephrosis).  The ureter dives under the uterine artery ("water under the bridge") in the cardinal ligaments at the site of uterine vessel ligation ((Figure 7)).  The uterine venous plexus drains into the internal iliac veins. ## Nerve supply The uterus receives autonomic innervation through the uterovaginal plexus as well as through sympathetic (via T10-L2) and parasympathetic fibers (S2-S4). ## Lymphatic drainage Lymph drainage of the uterus primarily occurs through the external iliac arteries, although some drainage (primarily of the fundus) occurs through the paraaortic lymph nodes. ## Histology The uterus is composed of 3 layers of tissue: - **Endometrium**:  The endometrium is the inner lining of the uterus and consists of the functional layer (shed during menstruation) and the regenerative basal layer.  The endometrial mucosa consists of endometrial glands (lined by columnar cells) with surrounding stroma.  The endometrium is dynamic, undergoing changes that are stimulated by estrogen and progesterone during phases of the menstrual cycle. - In the follicular phase (estrogen-dominant phase), the endometrium proliferates and thickens ((Figure 8)). - In the luteal phase (progesterone-dominant phase), the endometrium differentiates into secretory endometrium (via spiral vessel coiling and large intracytoplasmic glycogen vacuole deposition within the cells), preparing it for implantation ((Figure 9)).  If implantation does not occur, progesterone levels fall and the uterine lining sheds (menses). - **Myometrium**:  The myometrium comprises the majority of the uterus and is made of thick smooth muscle, which is responsible for uterine contractions during delivery. - **Perimetrium**:  The perimetrium is the outer serosal covering of the uterus, comprised of simple squamous epithelium. # Vagina The vagina is a fibromuscular tube (about 7-10 cm in length) and part of the outflow tract (for menstrual outflow, giving birth) of the female reproductive system.  The upper two-thirds of the vagina are formed from the paramesonephric ducts, and the lower one-third is formed from the urogenital sinus. ## Blood supply The primary blood supply of the vagina is the vaginal artery.  The origin of the vaginal artery varies and can arise from the internal iliac artery or the uterine artery.  The vaginal venous plexus drains into the internal iliac vein. ## Nerve supply Innervation of the vagina is varied and is divided according to embryologic origin.  The upper two-thirds are innervated by autonomic fibers from the uterovaginal plexus, whereas the lower one-third is innervated by somatic fibers from the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). ## Lymphatic drainage Lymph from the upper 2/3 of the vagina is drained to the internal iliac lymph nodes, whereas the lower one-third drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. ## Histology The vaginal wall is composed of 3 main layers: - **Mucosa**:  The mucosa is lined by nonkeratinized stratified epithelium, supported by a lamina propria rich in elastic and collagen fibers.  - **Muscularis**:  The muscularis is made up of 2 layers of smooth muscle (providing distensibility): the inner circular layer and the outer longitudinal layer. - **Adventitia**:  The adventitia is composed of connective tissue, which anchors the vagina to surrounding pelvic structures. # External genitalia (vulva) The external genitalia include the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, vestibule of the vagina, and greater vestibular glands ((Figure 10)).  Structures of the external genitalia are derived from the genital tubercule (eg, labia majora and minora, clitoris) and the urogenital sinus (eg, vaginal vestibule, greater vestibular glands). ## Blood supply The external genitalia receive blood from the internal pudendal artery, which arises from the internal iliac artery and travels from the pudendal canal with the pudendal nerve.  The internal pudendal vein drains into the internal iliac vein. ##
