# Cranial Nerves: Anatomy And Palsies

# Introduction

Cranial nerve palsies result from dysfunction of one or more of the 12 cranial nerves, leading to characteristic deficits depending on the affected nerve(s).  These deficits can arise from a wide range of structural, inflammatory, infectious, vascular, or neoplastic causes.  The clinical presentation varies based on the nerve involved, its anatomic course, and the underlying etiology.  Timely identification and diagnosis are essential for guiding management and mitigating complications.

# Overview of cranial nerves

Cranial nerves are paired structures.  Cranial nerves (CNs) III-XII originate in the brainstem at particular points along the midbrain, pons, and medulla, whereas CNs I and II originate in the cortex ((Video 1)).  All the cranial nerves have distinct sensory, motor, or mixed functions:

-   **Cranial nerve I (olfactory nerve)**:  Smell.
-   **Cranial nerve II (optic nerve)**:  Vision.
-   **Cranial nerve III (oculomotor nerve)**:  Eye movement, pupil constriction, and eyelid elevation.
-   **Cranial nerve IV (trochlear nerve)**:  Eye movement (superior oblique muscle).
-   **Cranial nerve V (trigeminal nerve)**: Facial sensation and mastication.
-   **Cranial nerve VI (abducens nerve)**: Eye abduction (lateral rectus muscle).
-   **Cranial nerve VII (facial nerve)**:  Facial expression, taste (anterior two-thirds of tongue), lacrimation, and salivation.
-   **Cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve)**:  Hearing and balance.
-   **Cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal nerve)**: Taste (posterior one-third of tongue), swallowing, and salivation.
-   **Cranial nerve X (vagus nerve)**:  Parasympathetic control of thoracic and abdominal organs, voice modulation, and swallowing.
-   **Cranial nerve XI (accessory nerve)**:  Shoulder elevation and head rotation.
-   **Cranial nerve XII (hypoglossal nerve)**:  Tongue movement.

The anatomy, function, testing, and pathology of each cranial nerve are discussed.

# Cranial nerve I (olfactory nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The olfactory nerve (CN I) carries special sensory fibers for the **perception of smell**, which is mediated by odorant molecules that bind to olfactory chemoreceptor cells in the nasal mucosa.  Axons of the chemoreceptor cells make up the olfactory nerve rootlets, which project through the **cribriform plate** of the ethmoid bone to synapse on the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb.  The olfactory bulb then projects second-order axons through the olfactory sulcus in the frontal lobes to the primary olfactory cortex in the medial temporal lobe via the olfactory tract.

## Palsy

**Anosmia** (absent sense of smell) can occur with dysfunction of CN I.  Patients often describe difficulties with taste, even though the taste sensation is intact, because the perception of flavor is dependent on both smell and taste, with smell being more important.  Anosmia is most often elicited in the history but can be formally tested with the placement of coffee or an alcohol pad under the nose.

Dysfunction of CN I typically occurs in the setting of **head trauma** (eg, with acceleration-deceleration forces), which can cause avulsion of the olfactory nerve rootlets as they traverse the cribriform plate ((Figure 1)).  Anosmia can also occur in Kallmann syndrome (characterized by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism), Parkinson disease (sometimes appearing before motor findings), and large tumors in the frontal lobe (eg, Foster Kennedy syndrome).

# Cranial nerve II (optic nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The optic nerve (CN II) carries **visual information** from the retinal ganglion cells in the eye and transmits this information to the brain via the visual pathway to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe ((Figure 2)).  CN II is also an important component of the pupillary light reflex; the reflex is mediated by afferents from CN II and efferents from the oculomotor nerve (CN III) to produce constriction of the pupils in response to light (see more details in the section on cranial nerve reflexes).

## Palsy

Testing of CN II includes several components: pupillary reflex, visual fields, visual acuity, and funduscopic examination.  Lesions in the optic nerve itself can cause:

-   **Relative afferent pupillary defect**:  When light is shined in the affected eye, no signal is transmitted, so pupillary constriction is equally impaired bilaterally ((Video 2)).
-   Central **monocular vision loss** demonstrated on visual acuity and visual field testing.
-   Difficulty with color vision (dyschromatopsia).
-   **Papilledema** or other abnormal funduscopic findings (eg, enlarged optic cup).

Dysfunction of CN II can occur in many conditions, including multiple sclerosis (eg, optic neuritis), infection (eg, syphilis), idiopathic intracranial hypertension, tumors (eg, optic glioma), open-angle glaucoma, or toxin-related optic neuropathy (eg, ethambutol).

# Cranial nerve III (oculomotor nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) has parasympathetic motor fibers:

-   The parasympathetic efferent fibers are located on the **periphery** and control **pupillary constriction** via the sphincter pupillae muscle.
-   The motor efferent fibers are located in the **interior** of the nerve and innervate **most extraocular muscles** (superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique) and the muscle that **elevates the upper eyelid** (levator palpebrae superioris).

CN III exits the midbrain between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, coursing along the posterior communicating artery.  It travels through the cavernous sinus and exits the skull via the superior orbital fissure.

## Palsy

CN III is tested by observing extraocular eye movements, the examiner standing approximately 0.6 m \[2 ft\] away and the patient avoiding head movement while following the examiner's finger in the horizontal and vertical directions.  In addition to the extraocular movements, the pupillary reflex and eyelid should be examined.  Lesions in the oculomotor nerve typically cause:

-   **"Down and out"** pupil due to paralysis of extraocular muscles with unopposed action of the superior oblique (innervated by CN IV) and lateral rectus (innervated by CN VI).
-   **Efferent pupillary defect**, which is an absent pupillary response in the affected eye when light enters either eye, or **mydriasis** (fixed, dilated pupil), due to complete paralysis of parasympathetic fibers ((Video 3)).
-   Ptosis (eg, drooping of the eyelid) due to paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris.

CN III palsy can be divided into non–pupil sparing (pupillary defect on examination) and pupil sparing (normal pupils on examination) etiologies; this is because parasympathetic fibers in the periphery are susceptible to compression but less impacted by ischemia:

-   **Non–pupil-sparing CN III palsies** are frequently caused by **mass effect** and should be considered due to an **intracranial aneurysm** (of the posterior communicating artery) until proved otherwise ((Figure 3)).  Patients should undergo immediate MRI or CT scan with angiography of the head for evaluation
-   **Pupil-sparing CN III palsies** are typically caused by **microvascular ischemia** and conditions such as **diabetes mellitus**, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and advanced age ((Figure 4)).  Observation and supportive care may be appropriate in patients with CN III palsy with vasculopathic risk factors.

# Cranial nerve IV (trochlear nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is a pure motor nerve that innervates the **superior oblique muscle**, **intorting (internally rotating) and depressing the eye while adducted**.  It exits at the level of the midbrain, travels through the cavernous sinus, and exits the skull at the superior orbital fissure, similar to CN III.

## Palsy

Patients with trochlear nerve palsy typically have vertical diplopia, which is most pronounced when the affected eye looks down and toward the nose (eg, up-close reading, descending stairs).  Examination may show impairment of downgaze with the eye in the adducted position.  In severe cases, the affected eye appears vertically deviated (hypertropia).  Symptoms often improve when the chin is tucked and the head is tilted away from the affected eye to compensate for hypertropia and extorsion ((Figure 5)).

Most cases of isolated CN IV palsy are due to congenital abnormalities.  Because of its long course and small caliber, CN IV palsy can also be acquired from head trauma; other cases may be due to microvascular nerve ischemia in the setting of diabetes mellitus or other vascular risk factors.

# Cranial nerve V (trigeminal nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The trigeminal nerve (CN V) provides **sensation to the face** and **motor innervation to the muscles of mastication** ((Figure 6)).  The trigeminal nerve exits from the pons and divides into 3 branches that then travel as follows ((Figure 7)):

-   **Ophthalmic nerve (CN V1)** passes through the cavernous sinus, exits the cranium through the superior orbital fissure, passes superiorly along the orbit, and then exits the orbit through the frontal bone via the supraorbital foramen.  This nerve supplies **sensation to the scalp, forehead, and eyes**.  Because it carries general sensory information from the eyes (including the cornea), it provides the afferent component of the **corneal reflex**.
-   **Maxillary nerve (CN V2)** passes through the cavernous sinus, leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum, and then traverses the pterygopalatine fossa to enter the maxilla via the infraorbital canal.  It then exits the facial bones through the infraorbital foramen to provide **sensation to the maxillary teeth, sinuses, and palate**.
-   **Mandibular nerve (CN V3)** exits the cranium through the foramen ovale ((Figure 8)).  This branch of CN V has several branches:
    -   One branch (the inferior alveolar nerve) enters the mandibular foramen on the internal surface of the mandible and then exits at the mental foramen at the anterior mandible; this provides **sensation to the lower teeth, chin, and lower lip**.
    -   **General sensation (not taste) in the anterior tongue** is carried by the lingual nerve.  It is also a branch of CN V3, but it arises proximal to the inferior alveolar nerve branch.
    -   The masseteric branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (CN V3) provides sensory innervation to the face and **motor innervation to the muscles of mastication**.  These include the muscles that close the jaw (masseter, medial pterygoid, temporalis) and the single muscle that opens the jaw (lateral pterygoid).
    -   The **jaw jerk reflex** has both afferent and efferent limbs carried through the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve ((Figure 9)).  As the only tendon reflex mediated above the plane of the foramen magnum, the pathologic presence of this reflex suggests bilateral lesions of the upper motor neuron pathways above the level of the pons (eg, multiple sclerosis, pseudobulbar palsy).

## Palsy

CN V is tested by checking light touch on the forehead, cheek, and chin on both sides of the face simultaneously.  Jaw strength can be tested with jaw opening and closing.  Damage to CN V can cause **ipsilateral facial anesthesia**, **loss of the corneal reflex**, **weakness of the muscles of mastication**, and **jaw deviation** toward the side of the lesion (due to unopposed action of the opposite pterygoid muscle).  Bilateral paralysis can cause mandibular drop and a lack of jaw movement.

Trigeminal neuralgia is one of the most common conditions involving CN V and typically causes sharp, shock-like pain lasting seconds to minutes along one of the branches (usually V2 or V3).  Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia is unusual and should prompt evaluation for other causes, including multiple sclerosis.  The inferior alveolar nerve of V3 is susceptible to iatrogenic injury during dental procedures.

# Cranial nerve VI (abducens nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The abducens nerve (CN VI) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which is responsible for **abduction of the eye**.  This nerve exits at the level of the pons, travels within the cavernous sinus, and subsequently exits the cranium via the superior orbital fissure, where it innervates the lateral rectus muscle.  It travels a long course, including through the subarachnoid space, which makes it prone to injury from increased cerebrospinal fluid pressure and stretching.

## Palsy

CN VI palsy is one of the most common nerve palsies that occurs in isolation.  Testing occurs as part of testing of extraocular eye movement (as noted in the section on CN III).  Palsies of this nerve can cause horizontal diplopia and inward deviation (esotropia).

The etiologies of CN VI palsy include a wide range of causes such as **increased intracranial pressure** (including from idiopathic intracranial hypertension), demyelination, ischemia, tumors, and infection (eg, meningitis), among other things.

# Cranial nerve VII (facial nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The facial nerve (CN VII) exits the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction near the cerebellopontine angle and subsequently enters the internal auditory meatus and facial canal in the temporal bone (traveling near the otic capsule and through the middle ear).  There, it branches, supplying the **stapedius muscle** (which reduces volume by dampening ossicle movement in the middle ear), **salivary glands** (eg, sublingual, submandibular), and **lacrimal glands**.  It also provides **taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue** via the chorda tympani nerve.  After exiting the skull through the stylomastoid foramen, the facial nerve courses within the parotid gland; its terminal branches innervate the **muscles of facial expression**.  This includes innervation of the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is the efferent limb of the **corneal reflex**.

## Palsy

CN VII is tested by having the patient close the eyes tightly (with the examiner attempting to manually open the eyes), wrinkle the forehead, and smile.  Facial nerve palsy presents with **ipsilateral facial paralysis** (eg, flattening of the nasolabial fold, drooping of the lower lip, inability to close the eye); there is also **loss of the corneal reflex**.  Paralysis of the stapedius muscle may lead to **increased sensitivity to sound** (hyperacusis).  Because the nerve to the stapedius is one of the first branches of the facial nerve, hyperacusis indicates that the facial nerve is injured near its brainstem origin.  Other features of CN VII palsy may include decreased lacrimation, salivation, and loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

The most common cause of facial nerve palsy is Bell palsy, which typically occurs idiopathically.  Trauma, infection (eg, Lyme disease), and tumors (eg, vestibular schwannomas, parotid gland tumors) can also occasionally cause facial nerve palsy.  Peripheral causes should be differentiated from central causes, as described in more detail in the article on facial palsy ((Figure 10)).

# Cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) exits the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle ((Figure 11)) at the junction of the pons and medulla and innervates structures in the inner ear; it carries information about **hearing**, **balance**, and **eye position** (via the vestibuloocular reflex \[VOR\]).

## Palsy

CN VIII is tested by determining whether patients can hear a finger rub near their ears and by observing gait and balance.  Weber and Rinne testing can help differentiate conductive from sensorineural hearing loss ((Table 1)).  Impairment of the cochlear portion of CN VIII leads to ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus (ringing in the ear), and damage to the vestibular portion causes unsteadiness and disequilibrium.  Nystagmus can also be present in dysfunction of CN VIII due to impairment of the VOR.

A common etiology of CN VIII palsy is a vestibular schwannoma, which arises from the vestibular portion of the nerve.  Dysfunction can also occur with vestibular neuritis, which typically presents with acute, sustained vertigo after a viral infection.

# Cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) originates in the medulla and exits the cranial cavity via the jugular foramen.  This nerve has numerous functions, including:

-   Motor:  Stylopharyngeus muscle, which **elevates the larynx during swallowing**.
-   Parasympathetic:  Parotid gland secretion.
-   General sensory:  Tympanic membrane (inner surface), eustachian tube, posterior third of tongue, tonsillar region, upper pharynx, carotid body, and carotid sinus.  These sensory fibers provide afferent information for both the gag reflex and the carotid sinus reflex.
-   **Taste in the posterior third of the tongue**.

## Palsy

CN IX is tested with CN X by asking the patient to say "aahh" and visualizing the movement of the palate.  Speech and swallowing can also be observed.  Although not routinely evaluated, the gag reflex is tested by touching the posterior pharynx with a cotton swab.  Glossopharyngeal nerve lesions result in loss of general sensation in the upper pharynx, posterior tongue, tonsils, and middle ear cavity; loss of the gag reflex (afferent limb); and loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue.

This nerve palsy rarely occurs in isolation, although it can develop after surgical procedures such as carotid endarterectomy and Eagle syndrome surgery.  It is commonly dysfunctional in lateral medullary syndrome.

# Cranial nerve X (vagus nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The vagus nerve (CN X) originates in the medulla and exits the cranial cavity via the jugular foramen.  It plays an important role in **swallowing**, **speech**, and **autonomic regulation** throughout the body.  The vagus nerve has several functions, including:

-   Motor:  Motor fibers innervate muscles of the soft palate, larynx, and pharynx.
-   General sensory:  Afferent (sensory) fibers innervate the larynx and hypopharynx.  Another branch that provides afferent sensory input from the external auditory canal.
-   Parasympathetic innervation to the major organs (eg, heart, lungs, gut).
-   Taste in the epiglottis and pharynx.

Given its motor and parasympathetic functions, CN X provides efferents for both the gag reflex and the carotid sinus reflex.  It is also responsible for the cough reflex.

## Palsy

Clinically, CN X is tested with CN IX (see previous section).  CN X injury causes loss of the efferent limb of the gag reflex (eg, soft palate dysfunction), dysphagia (eg, pharyngeal muscles), and hoarseness (eg, laryngeal muscles).  Sensory loss in the larynx and pharynx may also lead to impaired cough reflex.  
The vagus nerve is rarely injured in isolation; it is often impaired in lateral medullary syndrome or damaged during surgery (eg, thyroidectomy, carotid endarterectomy).  During thyroid surgery, the recurrent laryngeal nerve (a branch of the vagus nerve that loops below the aortic arch on the left and below the subclavian artery on the right) may be damaged due to its proximity to the inferior thyroid artery, causing hoarseness.  During fundiplication, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks (branches of the vagus nerve), which supply parasympathetic innervation to the gastrointestinal tract and stimulate gastric muscle contraction and motility, pass through the esophageal hiatus and are vulnerable to injury (eg, delayed gastric emptying).

# Cranial nerve XI (spinal accessory nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) is a pure motor nerve that innervates the **sternocleidomastoid** and **trapezius** muscles.  It arises from the cervical spinal cord, exits the cranium via the jugular foramen, and follows a superficial course through the posterior triangle of the neck ((Figure 12)).  The trapezius elevates and rotates the scapula upward (eg, during arm abduction) and stabilizes the shoulder.

## Palsy

CN XI can be tested by asking the patient to turn the head and shrug the shoulders against resistance.  Symptoms of trapezius weakness include drooping of the shoulder, impaired abduction of the arm above 100 degrees, and lateral displacement of the scapula.  If the injury involves the proximal portions of the nerve, weakness of the sternocleidomastoid muscle is also seen.

CN XI is vulnerable to penetrating trauma and iatrogenic injury (eg, cervical lymph node dissection) due to its superficial course in the neck.

# Cranial nerve XII (hypoglossal nerve)

## Nerve pathway and function

The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the medulla and travels through the hypoglossal canal to the angle of the mandible to reach the tongue.  It provides motor innervation to the tongue except for the palatoglossus muscle, which is innervated by the vagus nerve (CN X).

## Palsy

CN XII can be tested by asking patients to stick out the tongue, move it from side to side, and press it against the inside of the cheek against resistance.  CN XII injury causes tongue weakness; on tongue protrusion, the strong side "pushes" the tongue toward the weak side, sometimes remembered with the phrase "licking your wounds."

CN XII may be affected by a variety of disorders involving the medulla.  Because CN XII is primarily a motor nerve, tongue fasciculations and weakness are characteristic of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or spinal muscular atrophy, serving as helpful diagnostic clues.

# Essential cranial nerve reflexes

The cranial nerves play a role in several essential reflexes that can be tested if needed ((Table 2)).  Pupillary reflex testing can help localize disorders of the visual pathway; most of the other reflexes are tested as part of the brain death examination.  A few essential clinical reflexes are summarized.

## Pupillary reflex

During the normal pupillary reflex ((Figure 13)), the optic nerve (CN II) and tract (afferent fibers) transmit light stimulus to the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus, where it is received by the pretectal nucleus and subsequently relayed to the bilateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei.  These nuclei subsequently project preganglionic parasympathetic fibers (efferent fibers) through the oculomotor nerve (CN III) to the ciliary ganglion, which then projects postganglionic fibers that innervate the sphincter pupillae muscle to constrict the pupil.  When light is shined in one eye, both the ipsilateral pupil (direct response) and contralateral pupil (consensual response) constrict.

Defects in the pupillary reflex (afferent vs efferent) can help localize lesions:  The pupillary reflex is absent bilaterally in patients with brain death or severe midbrain dysfunction.

Note that **anisocoria** (ie, pupillary asymmetry) indicates a unilateral defect in input from either the ocular sympathetic (pupil dilation) or parasympathetic (pupil constriction) pathway.  In response to dim light, input from the oculosympathetic pathway initiates pupillary dilation, allowing more light to reach the retina.  Under bright light, parasympathetic input from the ipsilateral CN III initiates pupillary constriction, limiting the amount of light received by the retina.

-   Asymmetry that increases in dim light indicates that the smaller pupil is unable to dilate due to loss of sympathetic nerve input.  Under bright light, the asymmetry will decrease because parasympathetic input (pupillary constriction) is unaffected.
-   Asymmetry that increases under bright light indicates that the larger pupil is unable to constrict due to loss of parasympathetic nerve input.  In dim light, the asymmetry will decrease because sympathetic input (pupillary dilation) is unaffected.

## Corneal reflex

The sensory limb of the corneal reflex is mediated by the nasociliary branch of the first division of CN V1, which enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.  The motor component of the corneal reflex is carried primarily by the temporal branch of CN VII and triggers bilateral eye blinking.

To test the corneal reflex, the cornea is lightly touched with a cotton swab or stimulated with saline.  Absence of the corneal reflex (corneal stimulation causes orbicularis oculi to contract the eyelids) can result from lesions involving the afferent limb (CN V1) or efferent limb (CN VII).

## Vestibuloocular reflex

The VOR is responsible for compensatory eye movements with head movement.  CN VIII carries afferent vestibular information to the brainstem, whereas the cranial nerves responsible for eye movements (CN III, IV, and VI) provide efferents to the eye muscles.

The VOR can be tested in many ways.

-   In the conscious patient, the head impulse test for the VOR helps evaluate peripheral causes of vertigo.  In this test, the patient attempts to maintain focus on a distant target while the head is rapidly rotated left and then right.  Patients with normal vestibular function can keep their eyes on target.  However, patients with a peripheral vestibular lesion have their eyes pulled off target by head rotation toward the lesion, followed by a corrective saccade back to target.
-   In an unconscious patient, caloric testing or the oculocephalic reflex may be used to determine if the VOR is intact:
    -   In caloric testing, ice water is instilled in the ear canal.  If the reflex is intact, the eyes slowly move toward that ear.  If the reflex is absent, the eyes remain fixed.
    -   The oculocephalic reflex (eg, doll's-eye reflex) is tested by moving the head to the right and left and monitoring how the eyes move ((Figure 14)).  If the reflex is intact (indicating normal brainstem function), the eyes move in the opposite direction of the head to stay focused at the center.  If the reflex is absent (suggesting brainstem injury), the eyes remain fixed and stationary in the midline.

## Gag reflex

The gag reflex is an airway protective mechanism that acts to expel foreign or toxic material from the aerodigestive tract.  It is mediated by the following:

-   Sensory (afferent) signals from the back of the tongue or posterior pharyngeal wall are sent via CN IX.
-   Somatic sensory fibers of CN IX enter the brainstem at the medulla, descend along the spinal trigeminal tract, and synapse in the caudal spinal nucleus.
-   Information is then sent to the bilateral nuclei ambigui, which are located in the medulla.
-   Bilateral motor (efferent) signals are sent via CN X, elevating the soft palate and contracting the pharynx.

An absent gag reflex is suspicious for dysfunction of the medulla oblongata.

## Carotid sinus reflex

The carotid sinus is a dilation of the internal carotid artery located just above the bifurcation of the common carotid artery.  The carotid sinus reflex has an afferent limb that arises from the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and travels to the medullary centers via the Hering nerve, a branch of CN IX.  The efferent limb carries parasympathetic impulses via CN X ((Figure 15)).

Carotid sinus pressure or massage stimulates the baroreceptors and increases the firing rate from the carotid sinus, leading to an increase in parasympathetic output and withdrawal of sympathetic output to the heart and peripheral vasculature.  The result decreases blood pressure (via peripheral vasodilation) and decreases cardiac output (decreases contractility/stroke volume and heart rate).  In carotid sinus hypersensitivity, these effects can cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, and, sometimes, syncope.

# Syndromes with multiple cranial neuropathies

## Cavernous sinus syndrome

The dural sinuses are a venous network that drains blood from the brain into the internal jugular vein.  The cavernous sinus lies on each side of the sella turcica, posterior to the optic chiasm, and many important structures pass either through or within its walls, including the internal carotid artery, CNs III, IV, V1 and V2, and VI.

Infection, thrombosis, aneurysm (of the internal carotid artery), or trauma involving the cavernous sinus can damage these structures, leading to a syndrome with multiple cranial neuropathies.  Ocular muscle paralysis occurs due to injury of CNs III, IV, and VI.  CN III palsy may also result in ptosis and mydriasis.  Involvement of the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of CN V can cause loss of both upper facial sensation and the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.  Proptosis (eye protrusion) and chemosis (conjunctival swelling) may also be evident in venous thrombosis due to impaired venous drainage through the ophthalmic veins.  The cavernous sinus has anastomoses crossing the midline, so unilateral symptoms can rapidly become bilateral.

## Vestibular schwannoma

Vestibular schwannomas are the most common cause of cerebellopontine angle (ie, between the cerebellum and lateral pons) tumors in adults.  Vestibular schwannomas most often arise from the vestibular portion of CN VIII.  Spontaneous vestibular schwannomas are usually unilateral, whereas bilateral vestibular schwannomas are associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

CNs VII and V are in proximity to CN VIII at the cerebellopontine angle and may be compressed by vestibular schwannomas.  Symptoms can vary based on the pattern of nerve involvement:

-   Impairment of the cochlear portion of CN VIII leads to ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus (ringing in the ear), and damage to the vestibular portion causes unsteadiness and disequilibrium.
-   Compression of CN V may cause loss of ipsilateral facial sensation with interruption of the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.
-   CN VII compression can result in ipsilateral facial muscle paralysis (eg, asymmetric smile).

## Jugular foramen syndrome (eg, Vernet syndrome)

In several key foramina, the cranial nerves exit the skull ((Table 3)).  Damage to the cranial fossa bones can involve these foramina and cause specific symptoms.  The jugular foramen, formed by the petrous portion of the temporal bone and the occipital bone, is a large aperture in the base of the skull behind the carotid canal and is an important structure in the posterior cranial fossa.  Passing through the jugular foramina are CNs IX, X, and XI.

Lesions of the jugular foramen (eg, due to tumors, trauma, or infection) can result in jugular foramen syndrome, which is characterized by CN IX, X, and XI dysfunction:

-   Loss of taste from the posterior third of the tongue (CN IX).
-   Loss of gag reflex (CNs IX and X).
-   Dysphagia (CNs IX and X).
-   Dysphonia/hoarseness (CN X).
-   Soft palate drop with deviation of the uvula toward the normal side (CN X).
-   Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscle paresis (CN XI).

# Summary

Cranial nerve palsies result from dysfunction of one or more cranial nerves due to diverse causes, including ischemia, trauma, infections, and neoplasms.  The clinical presentation varies by nerve involvement, ranging from diplopia to facial weakness or hearing loss ((Table 4)).​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​

articles.title: Breast Anatomy And Histology
articles.markdown: # Breast Anatomy And Histology # Introduction A comprehensive understanding of breast anatomy is required for clinical practice, especially in the fields of surgery, oncology, and radiology.  The breast is a dynamic organ involved in lactation and hormonal responses. # Breast development In utero, the breasts develop from the **mammary ridge** (milk line), an ectodermal thickening that initially extends bilaterally from the axillae to the medial thighs; the remainder of the ridge subsequently regresses in early gestation. Occasionally, incomplete involution of the mammary ridge results in the formation of an accessory nipple (sometimes with associated glandular tissue) anywhere along this ridge ((Figure 1)).  The most common location of an accessory nipple is inferior to the breast.  Accessory nipples are usually asymptomatic, well-circumscribed, hyperpigmented papules that may become larger during puberty, before menses, or with pregnancy/lactation due to rising estrogen and progesterone levels (similar to physiologic changes in normal breast tissue).  Associated glandular tissue may also become tender or swollen. ## Puberty At birth, the breast rudiment contains 10-12 primitive glandular structures located beneath the nipple/areolar complex.  Prior to puberty, these ducts have very slow growth and branching.  For males, breast development halts at this stage.  For females, puberty marks the beginning of breast maturation (ie, thelarche) with an increase in stromal tissue and glandular development: The ducts proliferate and divide to form terminal end buds, which are transient structures that ultimately branch into small ductules called alveolar buds.  With further maturation and hormonal stimulation throughout the menstrual cycle (eg, via progesterone, estrogen), alveolar buds differentiate into the acinus, the terminal structure of the resting breast.  However, the breast does not reach full differentiation until pregnancy/lactation occurs. ## Pregnancy During pregnancy, additional branching occurs during the first trimester, and maximum glandular formation (ie, an increase in acini per terminal duct) and differentiation occur during the second and third trimesters.  The full extent of glandular differentiation is achieved with the formation of the secretory acinus, which is characterized by the ability to secrete milk proteins (caseins) and lipids. # Breast structure The adult breast is located in the superficial fascia of the anterior thoracic wall and is supported by **suspensory ligaments** (eg, Cooper ligaments).  It extends vertically from the 2nd rib to the 6th rib and laterally from the sternum to the midaxillary line.  The nipple is located centrally on the breast and is surrounded by the pigmented areola. The breast is composed of both stromal and epithelial tissue ((Figure 2)).  The stroma consists of fibrous connective tissue and adipose tissue and constitutes the majority of breast volume in nonlactating adult women.  Each breast is arranged into 15-20 **lobes** that radiate from the nipple, with intervening stromal tissue.  The lobes drain into a **major lactiferous duct** that converges into a **lactiferous sinus** beneath the areola to drain at the nipple.  Each lobe is further subdivided into lobules, which are composed of branched alveolar glands.  The structural and functional unit of the breast is the **terminal duct lobular unit**, each of which comprises the distal smallest duct (**terminal duct**) and the attached **acini** (mature alveolar glands). # Histology The entire ductal and lobular system of the breast is lined by 2 cell types.  The luminal aspect of the duct and acini contains columnar or cuboidal cells, whereas the outer cell layer is composed of spindle-shaped myoepithelial cells, which reside above the basement membrane.  The contractile myoepithelial cells are responsive to oxytocin and aid in milk ejection. # Blood supply The primary blood supply of the breast is the **internal mammary artery** (or internal thoracic artery), which originates from the subclavian artery.  Additional supply is through the lateral thoracic artery (also known as the external mammary artery), a branch of the axillary artery, which supplies primarily the upper, outer quadrants of the breast.  Venous drainage occurs primarily through the axillary vein. # Lymphatic drainage Lymphatic drainage occurs through both superficial and deep lymphatic vessels.  Lymph flows unidirectionally from the superficial system to the deep plexus.  Most of the lymph flow of the breasts drains to the **axillary lymph nodes** ((Figure 3)), although some can be directed to other nodes (eg, internal mammary nodes receive drainage medially, clavicular nodes receive drainage from the upper, outer quadrants of the breast).  Sampling of the lymphatic drainage of the breast helps determine metastatic spread of breast cancer. # Innervation The innervation of the breast comes primarily from the third, fourth, and fifth **intercostal nerves**.  The nipple receives highly concentrated innervation from the fourth intercostal nerve and typically lies at the level of the **T4 dermatome**. ​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌

# Brachial Plexus Injuries # Introduction Brachial plexus injuries involve damage to the network of nerves originating from the spinal cord that control motor and sensory functions in the shoulder, arm, and hand.  These injuries can result from trauma, obstetric complications, or compressive forces and can range in severity.  Prompt recognition and management are essential to optimize functional recovery. # Brachial plexus anatomy The brachial plexus ((Figure 1)) supplies all sensory and motor innervation to the upper extremities, except for an area of skin near the axilla (innervated by the intercostobrachial nerve) and the trapezius muscle (innervated by the accessory nerve \[CN XI\]).  It originates from the **C5-T1 spinal nerve roots**, which combine into **3 trunks** (superior, middle, and inferior); these pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles (scalene triangle) in the posterior neck ((Figure 2)).  The trunks then differentiate into divisions, cords, and terminal nerve branches ((Figure 3)).  Although there is significant overlap and redundancy throughout the cord, the primary functions of the plexus ((Table 1)) can be summarized into clinically relevant portions. ## Roots The C5-T1 nerve roots give rise to the 3 trunks of the brachial plexus.  Several smaller nerves also branch directly from the roots, including the dorsal scapular nerve (C5 root, which innervates the rhomboids to rotate the scapula) and the long thoracic (C5-C7 roots, which innervates the serratus anterior).  The roots also contribute fibers to the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), which innervates the diaphragm and carries pain fibers from the diaphragmatic and mediastinal pleura.  The C5-T1 roots also carry the sensory fibers that form the dermatomes of the upper extremities (C5 shoulder, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm). ## Trunks The roots combine to form the superior, middle, and inferior trunks: - **Superior trunk (C5-C6)**:  Contributes to the lateral and posterior cords, which supply muscles involved in shoulder abduction, external rotation, and elbow flexion.  It also gives rise to the suprascapular nerve, which innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus for initiation of abduction and external rotation. - **Middle trunk (C7)**:  Continues without major independent branches. - **Inferior trunk (C8-T1)**:  Contributes to the medial cord, which supplies much of the hand musculature. ## Cords The trunks separate into anterior and posterior divisions, which regroup as the lateral, posterior, and medial cords around the axillary artery. - **Lateral cord**:  Gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve and contributes to the median nerve. - **Posterior cord**:  Gives rise to the axillary nerve, radial nerve, and thoracodorsal nerve. - **Medial cord**:  Gives rise to the ulnar nerve and also contributes to the median nerve. ## Major nerve branches Several important nerves arise from the brachial plexus and provide motor and sensory innervation to the upper limb: - **Long thoracic nerve** (C5-C7):  Innervates the serratus anterior, which stabilizes and rotates the scapula upward, allowing complete abduction of the arm over the head. - **Musculocutaneous nerve** (C5-C7):  Innervates muscles that allow flexing at the elbow and supinating of the forearm (coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, brachialis).  It continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which supplies sensation to the lateral forearm. - **Axillary nerve** (C5-C6):  Innervates muscles that abduct the arm at the shoulder (deltoid) and assist with external rotation of the shoulder (teres minor).  It also carries sensation from the lateral shoulder. - **Thoracodorsal nerve** (C6-C8):  Innervates the latissimus dorsi, which extends, adducts, and internally rotates the humerus. - **Radial nerve** (C5-T1):  Innervates all the extensor muscles of the arm (below the shoulder) and hand and provides sensory innervation to the skin of the posterior arm, forearm, and dorsal lateral hand. - **Median nerve** (C5-T1):  Innervates muscles involved in wrist and finger flexion and thumb opposition/abduction (thenar muscles).  It also carries sensation from the palmar surface of the first three digits and radial half of the fourth digit. - **Ulnar nerve** (C8-T1):  Innervates muscles involved in flexion and adduction at the wrist, as well as fine motor control of most intrinsic hand muscles.  It also carries sensation from the fifth digit and medial half of the fourth digit. Of note, the second-order neurons in the oculosympathetic pathway, which arise from the C8-T2 levels of the spinal cord, also ascend through the brachial plexus. # Pathophysiology and risk factors Injury to the brachial plexus can occur due to a variety of underlying causes, including: - Direct nerve injury, such as from trauma (eg, clavicular or humerus fracture, penetrating injury). - Excessive traction on the nerves, most commonly due to traction during delivery.  Infants with shoulder dystocia are at increased risk, although it can occur in uncomplicated deliveries as well. - Compression from tumors or improper arm positioning. - Damage from surgical or radiation treatment for cancer. # Clinical presentation The presentation of brachial plexus injuries varies by the anatomical level of injury, and the pattern of deficits can help guide the diagnosis, work-up, and management.  The patterns of the most common injuries are discussed here. # Upper plexus injury (eg, Erb-Duchenne palsy) Erb-Duchenne palsy is the most common type of brachial plexus injury and usually involves the **superior trunk**, which is formed from the fifth (C5) and sixth (C6) cervical nerves that contribute primarily to the axillary, musculocutaneous, and radial nerves.  Erb-Duchenne palsy is most associated with shoulder dystocia, which occurs when the fetal shoulder becomes impacted behind the pubic symphysis during delivery, possibly resulting from excessive traction on the head and neck and injury to the brachial plexus nerve roots. Infants with Erb-Duchenne palsy experience ((Figure 4)): - Weakness of the deltoid (arm abduction) and infraspinatus muscles (external rotation), innervated by C5. - Weakness of the biceps (elbow flexion), brachioradialis (forearm supination), wrist extensors, innervated by C6. - In some patients, the **middle trunk** with the C7 nerve root is also involved, leading to weak finger extension and fingers held in a flexed position. - Patients typically have decreased or absent Moro and biceps reflexes due to weakness of the upper arm muscles, but the grasp reflex remains intact. This pattern of weakness leads to predominance of the opposing muscles, which results in the affected arm being held in adduction and internal rotation with the forearm pronated and the wrist flexed.  The resulting appearance with severe injury is the characteristic **waiter's tip posture**. Management of infants with Erb-Duchenne palsy involves observation and physical therapy because up to 80% of patients have spontaneous recovery within 3 months.  Prognosis depends on whether the damage results from mild nerve stretching or compression as opposed to severe rupture or avulsion.  Surgical intervention (eg, nerve graft, reconstruction, decompression) can be considered for infants with no improvement by age 3-9 months but is not necessarily curative. # Lower plexus injury Injuries to the lower brachial plexus typically affect the **inferior trunk**, which carries nerve fibers from the C8 and T1 spinal levels that ultimately contribute to the median and ulnar nerves.  Injuries to the lower plexus can cause: - Weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hands (eg, lumbricals and impaired flexion of the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension of the interphalangeal joints). - Sensory loss of the medial aspect of the hand (C8) and/or forearm (T1). - Concomitant Horner syndrome (eg, ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) due to associated damage to the sympathetic fibers that run along C8 and T1. The causes of lower plexus injuries are variable.  Klumpke palsy caused by trauma, thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), and compression from Pancoast tumors are discussed here. ## Klumpke palsy Klumpke palsy is an injury to the lower portion of the brachial plexus typically caused by shoulder dystocia during delivery ((Figure 5)) and less commonly from traumatic, sudden upward jerking of the arm at the shoulder ((Figure 6)).  This injury can cause the features described above; patients with significant injury can present with the total **claw hand deformity** ((Figure 7)). In newborns with Klumpke palsy from delivery, prognosis depends on whether the damage was due to nerve stretching or compression as opposed to avulsion.  Horner syndrome portends a suboptimal outcome.  Treatment usually involves gentle massage and physical therapy to prevent contractures.  In most cases, function returns within a few months.  If no improvement is seen by age 3-9 months, surgical intervention may be considered. ## Thoracic outlet syndrome Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a condition that occurs when the neurovascular bundle (consisting of the brachial plexus, subclavian artery, and subclavian vein) is compressed within the confined space between the clavicle and first rib (ie, thoracic outlet) ((Figure 8)).  TOS can be venous, arterial, or neurogenic, with neurogenic TOS responsible for >95% of cases.  Patients with TOS typically have a history of trauma (eg, clavicular fracture) or repetitive overhead arm movements (eg, swimming).  The presence of an anomalous cervical rib or scalene muscular anomalies can predispose to TOS. Symptoms of neurogenic TOS often affect the lower plexus (eg, C8 and T1 nerve roots) because the inferior portion of the brachial plexus is more easily compressed, particularly during activities that require repetitive overhead arm movements (eg, swimming, stacking boxes).  Clinically, patients often primarily have numbness or dysesthesia, often primarily in the T1 dermatome.  In later stages, weakness and atrophy of the muscles of the hand (particularly in the thumb) and forearm can be present.  Horner syndrome is rare on initial presentation. Symptoms of TOS may resolve completely with rest.  Reproduction of symptoms with raising the arm overhead is classic.  Initial management is typically TOS-specific physical therapy.  If the subclavian vein and/or artery is involved, patients may present with ischemia or deep vein thrombosis, which should be managed urgently. ## Pancoast syndrome Pancoast tumors are usually non–small cell lung cancers (eg, squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma) that arise near the superior sulcus (groove produced by the subclavian artery).  Due to their unique anatomic location, Pancoast tumors invade extrapulmonary structures near the lung apex ((Figure 9)).  They produce a collection of symptoms and signs called Pancoast syndrome, which include symptoms that occur due to invasion of the lower brachial plexus (eg, C8 and T1 nerve roots): - Shoulder pain or pain in the medial aspect of the forearm and arm (eg, C8-T1 dermatomes).  Pain from a Pancoast tumor may also be from referred pain from invasion of the first and second ribs or parietal pleura.  This symptom occurs in up to 95% of patients with Pancoast tumors. - Weakness or atrophy of the intrinsic hand muscles. - Horner syndrome (eg, ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) due to invasion of the paravertebral sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion. Other complications of a Pancoast tumor include superior vena cava syndrome (face/arm edema), phrenic nerve invasion (hemidiaphragm elevation), and recurrent laryngeal neuropathy (hoarseness). # Isolated major branch injuries ## Long thoracic nerve injury The long thoracic nerve arises from the C5-C7 roots and innervates the serratus anterior, which stabilizes and rotates the scapula upward.  Injury causes paralysis of the muscle, leading to scapular winging due to the inability of the serratus to hold the scapula against the thorax.  Patients also demonstrate weakness with arm abduction above the horizontal position due to impaired rotation of the scapula.  It most commonly occurs after axillary lymph node dissection or chest tube placement. ## Musculocutaneous nerve injury The musculocutaneous nerve arises from the lateral cord and innervates the coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis muscles.  Damage results in weakness of elbow flexion and forearm supination, often with an absent biceps reflex and sensory loss over the lateral forearm.  Common mechanisms of injury include shoulder dislocation or strenuous activity such as baseball pitching. ## Radial nerve injury The radial nerve arises from the posterior cord and innervates the extensor muscles of the arm and forearm.  Injury produces weakness with wrist and finger extension (wrist drop) and sensory loss over the posterior arm, posterior forearm, and dorsolateral hand.  Midshaft humeral fractures and penetrating trauma in the axilla are common causes. ## Median nerve injury The median nerve arises from the medial and lateral cords and innervates most forearm flexors and the thenar muscles.  It courses with the brachial artery between the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles before entering the forearm.  In the anterior (volar) forearm, it passes between the heads of the pronator teres before coursing between the flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus muscles.  It ultimately passes into the hand through the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum.  Injury causes weakness with wrist and finger flexion and loss of thumb opposition and abduction, with sensory loss in the palmar surface of the first three digits and radial half of the fourth digit.  Common mechanisms include supracondylar humeral fracture in children and carpal tunnel syndrome in adults. ## Ulnar nerve injury The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord and innervates the flexor carpi ulnaris, medial flexor digitorum profundus, and most intrinsic hand muscles.  It is commonly injured by trauma or nerve compression at the elbow (funny bone) or at Guyon canal (eg, striking the ground during a fall).  Injury at Guyon canal causes sensory loss in the medial 1½ digits along with intrinsic hand weakness.  The hypothenar eminence can appear flattened due to atrophy of denervated muscles.  Weakness of the lumbricals in the fourth/fifth digits may also produce an ulnar claw appearance during finger extension.  Injury at the elbow will cause similar symptoms along with sensory loss in the hypothenar eminence (palmar cutaneous branch) and medial dorsum of the hand (dorsal cutaneous branch).  Weakness on wrist flexion/adduction (flexor carpi ulnaris) and flexion of the fourth/fifth digits (medial portion of flexor digitorum profundus) may also be present. ## Thoracodorsal nerve injury The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord and innervates the latissimus dorsi, which extends, adducts, and internally rotates the humerus.  Injury results in weakness with arm adduction, extension, and internal rotation.  This nerve is particularly vulnerable during axillary surgery or repetitive overhead sports (eg, throwing, swinging). # Diagnosis In brachial plexus injuries, nerve conduction studies with electromyography as well as imaging with MRI or CT myelography are often performed to confirm a lesion localized to the brachial plexus. # Management Management of brachial plexus depends on the etiology.  For most brachial plexus injuries, management usually involves physical therapy to improve function; improvement is often noted within the first 6 months of therapy.  If improvement is limited, surgical interventions (eg, nerve grafts or transfers) may be considered. # Differential diagnosis Differential diagnoses for brachial plexus injuries and lesions to the terminal branches include: - **Cervical radiculopathy**:  Presents with sensory deficits and weakness in specific dermatomes, often with neck pain, and is often the result of disc herniation. - **Peripheral nerve injuries**:  Present with weakness and sensory changes localized to a specific nerve (eg, radial or ulnar nerve). - **Rotator cuff pathology**:  Presents with shoulder weakness with preserved elbow and hand function and positive impingement tests. # Summary Brachial plexus injuries involve a spectrum of nerve damage affecting motor and sensory function in the upper extremeties.  Traumatic and obstetric causes are most common, and the clinical presentation varies with the level and type of injury.  Management typically involves physical therapy with surgical interventions for refractory cases. ​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌

articles.title: Basic Blood Cell Types: Erythrocytes, Leukocytes, And Platelets
articles.markdown: # Basic Blood Cell Types: Erythrocytes, Leukocytes, And Platelets # Introduction Blood is a specialized connective tissue containing various cell types suspended in plasma, each originating from multipotent hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow.  This article reviews the basic types of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells (composed of granulocytes and agranulocytes), and platelets.  Morphologic characteristics, functional roles, and common pathologic alterations are discussed.  Hematopoiesis and cell lineages are explored in detail in a separate article. # Red blood cells Red blood cells (RBCs), or erythrocytes, are the most abundant blood cells, accounting for approximately 40%-45% of blood volume ((Figure 1)).  Their primary functions are to transport **oxygen** from the lungs to the tissues and to return carbon dioxide to the lungs for exhalation.  Measuring 6-8 µm in diameter, RBCs are uniquely biconcave in shape, increasing the surface area available for efficient gas exchange.  Gas exchange is facilitated by **hemoglobin**, an iron-containing protein that binds oxygen.  RBCs **lack a nucleus** and organelles, allowing more space for hemoglobin but limiting them to a **120-day lifespan** before they are recycled by the spleen and liver.  Erythropoiesis, the differentiation of RBCs from early progenitor cells, is stimulated primarily by erythropoietin produced by the kidneys.  RBC pathology includes: - Anemia:  Reduced RBC count or hemoglobin level decreases oxygen delivery. - Polycythemia:  Excessive RBC production increases blood viscosity, predisposing to thrombosis. - Sickle cell disease:  Abnormal hemoglobin distorts RBCs into a characteristic sickle shape, leading to vascular occlusion, hemolysis, and tissue damage. - Thalassemia:  Decreased hemoglobin alpha- or beta-chain production results in abnormal polymers that cause ineffective erythropoiesis and chronic hemolysis. # Granulocytes Granulocytes are a category of white blood cell (WBC) (leukocyte) characterized by cytoplasmic granules and a lobed nucleus that rapidly respond to injury or infection as a part of the **innate immune response**.  They include neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils, each containing specialized, preformed granules loaded with enzymes and inflammatory mediators for rapid defensive responses.  Their production and activation are tightly regulated by specific colony-stimulating factors (eg, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) and interleukins. ## Neutrophils Neutrophils (10-12 µm) are the most abundant granulocytes (comprising approximately 60% of WBCs) and contain **multilobed nuclei** (2-5 lobes) ((Figure 2)).  The nuclear segmentation increases as neutrophils mature, with young neutrophils having band-shaped (less segmented) nuclei.  This segmental nature of the nuclei is the reason that mature neutrophils are sometimes referred to as polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Neutrophils serve as first responders to **bacterial infections**, rapidly mobilizing to sites of invasion, where they phagocytize (ie, engulf) pathogens.  Their segmented nucleus allows neutrophils to squeeze through tight spaces in blood vessel walls (diapedesis) to reach infection sites without damaging their DNA ((Figure 3)).  This nuclear architecture also positions chromatin toward the cell periphery, maximizing central cytoplasmic space available for phagocytosis.  Their characteristic neutral-staining granules contain powerful destructive enzymes, including **myeloperoxidase** and lysozyme. For example, in a patient with pneumonia, neutrophils are recruited from the systemic circulation by chemokines and are subsequently activated by microbial molecules (eg, lipopolysaccharide, peptidoglycan, bacterial DNA) and opsonizing factors (eg, IgG, complement) to phagocytize and destroy the pathogenic bacteria.  Activated neutrophils also release cytotoxic granules (lysosomes) containing myeloperoxidase and other digestive enzymes that destroy extracellular bacteria and recruit additional immune components to the area.   However, these enzymes also cause significant damage to the pulmonary parenchyma and can result in liquefying necrosis of lung tissue and (potentially) lung abscess. Increased neutrophil counts (neutrophilia) are seen in infection or inflammation.  Decreased neutrophil counts (neutropenia) can occur due to various reasons—including chemotherapy, severe infections, and vitamin B12/folate deficiency—increasing susceptibility to infections. ## Eosinophils Eosinophils (12-17 µm) comprise approximately 2%-4% of WBCs and contain bilobed nuclei, resembling a pair of connected lobes ((Figure 4)).  This bilobed nuclear structure facilitates cellular mobility and flexibility, allowing eosinophils to migrate efficiently into inflamed tissues.  Their prominent eosinophilic (red-orange staining) granules contain cytotoxic molecules (eg, **major basic protein**, eosinophil peroxidase) optimized for combating **parasitic** infections by disrupting pathogen cell membranes.  Eosinophil proliferation and activation is stimulated by IL-5 produced by TH2 and mast cells (not to be confused with IL-4, which stimulates IgE production).  When a parasite invades the mucosa or enters the bloodstream, it is coated by IgG and IgA antibodies that bind the Fc receptors located on the eosinophil cell surface.  This triggers eosinophil degranulation and release of cytotoxic proteins and reactive oxygen intermediates, substances that damage and destroy antibody-bound parasites.  This mechanism is an example of antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, which is also used by macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer cells. Eosinophils also regulate **allergic** reactions by modulating inflammatory responses.  They synthesize prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and cytokines that contribute to the inflammation seen in late-phase type 1 hypersensitivity and chronic allergic reactions. Increased eosinophil counts (eosinophilia) suggest an allergic process (eg, asthma, hay fever), parasitic infection (eg, helminths such as *Ascaris* \[Loffler syndrome, intestinal obstruction\] and *Angiostrongylus* \[eosinophilic meningitis\]), drug reaction (eg, DRESS \[**D**rug **R**eaction with **E**osinophilia and **S**ystemic **S**ymptoms\]), or certain autoimmune disorders (eg, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis). ## Basophils Basophils (12-15 µm), the rarest granulocytes (comprising <1% of WBCs), have bilobed nuclei often obscured by dense, dark purple granules ((Figure 5)).  These large granules store **histamine** and heparin, critical mediators of allergic reactions and inflammation.  The basophil's granule-packed cytoplasm enables rapid, controlled release of histamine to induce **vasodilation** and enhance immune cell access to affected tissues, facilitating a prompt inflammatory response.  Increased basophil counts (basophilia) are rare but can be seen in certain types of malignancy (eg, chronic myeloid leukemia, myeloproliferative disorders). # Agranulocytes Agranulocytes, another category of WBCs, lack prominent cytoplasmic granules compared to granulocytes and are critical for **cell-mediated immunity** and antigen recognition.  They consist of lymphocytes and monocytes. ## Lymphocytes Lymphocytes (6-15 µm), constituting an estimated 20%-40% of WBCs, typically feature a large, round nucleus surrounded by a narrow rim of basophilic cytoplasm ((Figure 6)).  This **high nucleus/cytoplasm ratio** allows for the storage of a **large amount of genetic information** essential for generating **adaptive immunity** processes (eg, antigen recognition, immune memory).  Subtypes include **B cells** (producing specific antibodies through plasma cell differentiation), **T cells** (targeting infected or cancerous cells through cytotoxicity or helper functions), and **natural killer cells** (recognizing and eliminating virus-infected cells via perforin and granzyme release).  Lymphocyte differentiation is driven by antigen exposure and cytokines (eg, IL-2, IL-7) that stimulate maturation into effector or memory cells (with heightened response capabilities on reexposure). Lymphocytosis can be seen in viral infections and lymphoid malignancies (eg, chronic lymphocytic leukemia).  In contrast, lymphopenia is seen in immunodeficiencies and, occasionally, certain viral infections (eg, HIV, COVID-19). ## Monocytes Monocytes (12-20 µm), comprising approximately 3%-8% of WBCs, contain large, irregularly shaped, kidney-bean nuclei with **abundant gray-blue cytoplasm** ((Figure 7)).  Their expansive cytoplasmic volume facilitates **phagocytosis** of pathogens and debris.  On migration into tissues, monocytes differentiate into **macrophages and dendritic cells**—specialized antigen-presenting cells crucial for coordinating immune responses by processing and presenting antigens to T cells.  The differentiation of monocytes is promoted by macrophage colony-stimulating factor. Monocytosis can be seen in chronic infections (particularly bacterial infections \[eg, tuberculosis\]), chronic inflammatory conditions (eg, sarcoidosis), and certain malignancies (eg, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, acute monocytic leukemia).  In contrast, monocytopenia is less common but may occur in hairy cell leukemia and as an adverse effect of certain medications (eg, chemotherapy agents). # Platelets Platelets (thrombocytes) are the **smallest** blood cells (2-4 µm) and are irregularly shaped fragments derived from **megakaryocytes** in the bone marrow ((Figure 8)).  Their differentiation is regulated primarily by thrombopoietin produced by the liver.  The small size of platelets and the **lack of nuclei** optimize rapid circulation and facilitate quick adhesion to damaged vessel walls, forming initial **platelet plugs**.  Platelets contain numerous **granules filled with clotting factors** (eg, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor) and growth factors (eg, platelet-derived growth factor), enabling prompt secretion on activation to stabilize blood clots and promote tissue healing.  With a **7- to 10-day lifespan**, their production and function are tightly regulated to prevent excessive bleeding or clotting. Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) increases the risk for bleeding.  Thrombocytosis (high platelets) may lead to thrombosis.  Platelet dysfunction (eg, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann thrombasthenia) impairs clotting, even in the setting of normal counts, due to molecular defects in platelet adhesion or aggregation. # Summary Blood consists of 3 main cell types, each with specialized functions. Red blood cells (erythrocytes), the most abundant blood cells, are responsible for oxygen transport via hemoglobin.  Common disorders include anemia (low red blood cell count), polycythemia (excess red blood cells), and sickle cell disease (abnormal hemoglobin). White blood cells (leukocytes) are key to immunity and are divided into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes).  Neutrophils fight bacterial infections, eosinophils combat parasites and allergies, and basophils release histamine in allergic responses.  Lymphocytes (B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells) mediate adaptive immunity, whereas monocytes mature into macrophages and dendritic cells, aiding in pathogen clearance.  Abnormal white blood cell counts can indicate infections, inflammation, or malignancies. Platelets are small cell fragments essential for clotting; imbalances can lead to bleeding disorders (thrombocytopenia) or excessive clotting (thrombocytosis). ​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌
