# Anatomy: Wrist # Introduction The wrist is the joint connecting the forearm and the hand.  It allows the transfer of forces across the joint while permitting a wide range of motion for the hand.  It is composed of a stable bony framework with ligaments, tendons, muscles, and nerves, whose organization influences how wrist conditions (eg, due to compression, degeneration, or trauma) present clinically. # Skeleton and joints The wrist skeleton consists of the distal radius and ulna (joined at the distal radioulnar joint \[DRUJ\]) proximally and the 8 carpal bones (arranged in proximal and distal rows) distally ((Figure 1)), ((Figure 2)). ## Distal radioulnar joint The DRUJ is an articulation between the distal radius and ulna, stabilized by the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).  It allows pronation and supination of the forearm and is functionally distinct from the carpal joints.  It is critical for coordinated hand positioning and load transmission during grip and manipulation. ## Proximal carpal row The 4 proximal carpal row bones (laterally to medially) are the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, and pisiform.  The **scaphoid** bridges both carpal rows, functioning as the link for force transmission between the forearm and the hand.  The **pisiform** is a unique sesamoid bone embedded in the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) tendon; it functions primarily as a mechanical pulley and ligament attachment site, contributing to the medial boundary of the Guyon canal. ## Distal carpal row The 4 distal carpal row bones (laterally to medially) are the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate.  The bones interlock tightly, forming a stable platform for the metacarpal bases. The midcarpal joint separates the 2 rows and contributes most to wrist flexion and extension.  Together, the carpal bones form an intercalated segment system with no direct muscular attachments; this arrangement allows complex, synchronized motion but makes the wrist uniquely susceptible to instability patterns. # Ligaments The wrist is stabilized by a network of intrinsic and extrinsic ligaments.  Intrinsic ligaments connect carpal bones to each other; extrinsic ligaments connect the radius or ulna to the carpal bones.  Certain ligaments are particularly important for maintaining carpal stability and proper wrist function. ## Extrinsic ligaments - **Volar radiocarpal ligaments** (especially the radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments):  These are the most important extrinsic stabilizers.  They connect the radius to the scaphoid, lunate, and capitate and are essential for guiding and constraining carpal motion. - **Dorsal radiocarpal ligaments**:  These ligaments coordinate coupled motion during flexion.  They also contribute to stability. - **Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments**:  These provide lateral stability by limiting radial and ulnar deviation, respectively. ## Intrinsic ligaments - **Scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL)**:  This is the most important intrinsic ligament.  It is the critical stabilizer of the scapholunate joint and maintains overall carpal stability. - **Lunotriquetral ligament**:  This important stabilizer of the proximal carpal row connects the lunate with the triquetrum. ## Triangular fibrocartilage complex The TFCC is a separate, specialized structure on the ulnar side of the wrist comprised of an articular disc, the palmar and dorsal radioulnar ligaments, the ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral ligaments, and the extensor carpi ulnaris subsheath.  It stabilizes the DRUJ and ulnar carpus, facilitates smooth pronation-supination, and absorbs ulnar-sided load.  Injury to TFCC ligaments disrupts carpal mechanics and can lead to instability and arthritis. # Muscles and tendons The muscles controlling the wrist are organized into flexor (volar) and extensor (dorsal) compartments.  They work together to produce wrist motion and maintain stability. ## Flexors (anterior compartment) - **Flexor carpi radialis (FCR)**:  Originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus; inserts at the base of the second metacarpal; flexes and radially deviates the wrist. - **FCU**:  Originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and olecranon; inserts on the pisiform, hook of hamate, and base of the fifth metacarpal; flexes and ulnarly deviates the wrist. - **Palmaris longus**:  Originates from the medial epicondyle; inserts into the palmar aponeurosis and flexor retinaculum; assists wrist flexion. - **Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS)**:  Originates from the medial epicondyle, radius, and ulna; inserts on the middle phalanges of fingers 2-5; contributes to wrist and finger flexion (proximal interphalangeal joint). - **Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP)**:  Originates from the proximal ulna and interosseous membrane; inserts on the distal phalanges of fingers 2-5; flexes the wrist and fingers (at the distal interphalangeal joint \[DIP\]) ((Figure 3)), ((Table 1)). ## Extensors (posterior compartment) - **Extensor carpi radialis longus**:  Originates from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus; inserts at the base of the second metacarpal; extends and radially deviates the wrist. - **Extensor carpi radialis brevis**:  Originates from the lateral epicondyle; inserts at the base of the third metacarpal; extends the wrist and assists radial deviation. - **Extensor carpi ulnaris**:  Originates from the lateral epicondyle and posterior ulna; inserts at the base of the fifth metacarpal; extends and ulnarly deviates the wrist. - **Extensor digitorum**:  Originates from the lateral epicondyle; inserts on the extensor expansions of fingers 2-5; extends the wrist and fingers. - **Extensor indicis**:  Originates from the posterior ulna; inserts on the extensor expansion of the index finger; extends the index finger and assists wrist extension. - **Extensor digiti minimi**:  Originates from the lateral epicondyle; inserts on the extensor expansion of the little finger; extends the little finger and assists wrist extension ((Figure 4), ((Table 2)). Together, these flexor and extensor muscles coordinate wrist motion, stabilize the joint, and facilitate complex hand movements. # Fascial anatomy The wrist is enveloped by the superficial antebrachial fascia; 2 major stabilizing structures lie deep to it: the flexor retinaculum on the volar side and the extensor retinaculum on the dorsal side ((Figure 5)): - **Flexor retinaculum** (ie, transverse carpal ligament):  Forms the carpal tunnel, transmitting the median nerve and 9 flexor tendons.  Because it forms a rigid fibroosseous tunnel, swelling of the tendon sheaths or subsynovial connective tissue can increase pressure and produce median nerve compression. - **Extensor retinaculum**:  Anchors 6 dorsal tendon compartments, each containing specific extensor tendons with associated synovial sheaths.  These compartments prevent tendon bowstringing and form closed spaces where tenosynovitis or infection may localize. These retinacula serve as major anatomic boundaries that partition the wrist into discrete functional spaces. # Synovial compartments and deep spaces ## Flexor tendon sheaths Flexor tendons are invested in synovial sheaths that facilitate gliding.  The 2 largest—the radial bursa (flexor pollicis longus \[FPL\]) and ulnar bursa (FDS/FDP to the little finger)—may communicate in the palm.  This communication creates predictable pathways for infections (eg, flexor tenosynovitis), which can track into the radial or ulnar bursae or form a horseshoe abscess (infection in one finger leading to infection on the opposite side of the hand). ## Extensor compartments Each extensor compartment on the dorsum of the wrist possesses its own synovial sheath, which can become inflamed in overuse conditions (eg, de Quervain tenosynovitis). ## Joint spaces The radiocarpal, midcarpal, and carpometacarpal joints contain synovial cavities that may be involved in septic arthritis, inflammatory synovitis, or posttraumatic effusions.  Because they are bound by strong capsuloligamentous structures, infection and fluid spread are often contained and produce localized swelling. ## Vessels The wrist receives its blood supply from both the radial and the ulnar arteries, which form anastomotic networks around the carpal bones ((Figure 6)). ## Radial artery The radial artery courses laterally down the forearm and, at the wrist, divides into the following: - **Superficial palmar branch** (contributing to the superficial palmar arch). - **Deep palmar branch** (forming the deep palmar arch). - **Dorsal carpal branch** (forming the dorsal carpal arch). The deep palmar branch passes through the first dorsal interosseous space to join the deep branch of the ulnar artery, whereas the dorsal carpal branch anastomoses with the dorsal carpal branch of the ulnar artery to form the dorsal carpal arch. ## Ulnar artery The ulnar artery runs medially and divides into the following: - **Palmar carpal branch** (forming the palmar carpal arch with the radial palmar carpal branch). - **Superficial branch** (primarily forming the superficial palmar arch). - **Deep branch** (joining the deep palmar arch). The ulnar artery is typically the dominant contributor to the superficial palmar arch, whereas the deep palmar arch is most often completed by the radial artery. Venous drainage typically parallels arterial flow.  These anastomoses provide robust collateral circulation, which is clinically significant for maintaining hand perfusion even if a single artery is compromised. # Nerves The wrist is innervated by branches of the median, ulnar, and radial nerves. ## Median nerve - **Course**:  Passes through the carpal tunnel deep to the flexor retinaculum, just radial to the midline of the wrist.  The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel (supplying sensation to the central palm); the main trunk continues into the hand ((Figure 7)). - **Motor**: - Supplies most volar forearm muscles that cross the wrist: - FCR:  Deviates wrist flexor and radial deviator (primary function). - Palmaris longus:  Assists wrist flexion. - FDS:  Contributes to wrist and finger flexion. - Supplies most thenar muscles and the lateral 2 lumbricals. - **Sensory**:  Supplies the palmar surface of the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger ((Figure 8)). ## Ulnar nerve - **Course**:  Passes superficially to the flexor retinaculum through the Guyon canal, ulnar to the carpal tunnel.  Divides at the wrist into the superficial and deep branches ((Figure 9)). - **Motor**: - FCU:  Wrist flexion and adduction. - FDP (ulnar half; digits 4-5):  Wrist flexion and DIP finger flexion. - Most intrinsic hand muscles (deep branch) (including hypothenar muscles, interossei, adductor pollicis, and medial lumbricals). - **Sensory**:  Dorsal and palmar superficial branches supply sensation to the ulnar side of the hand (including the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger) and wrist ((Figure 10)). ## Radial nerve - **Course**:  Bifurcates in the proximal forearm into: - **Superficial radial nerve (sensory)**:  Runs subcutaneously along the radial aspect of the forearm and crosses the wrist dorsolaterally, superficial to the wrist capsule. - **Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) (motor)**:  Enters the supinator and travels along the dorsal forearm.  The PIN divides into articular branches to the dorsal radiocarpal joint, the TFCC, and the DRUJ ((Figure 11)). - **Motor (via the PIN)**:  Supplies the major wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor carpi radialis longus \[before the bifurcation\]). - **Sensory (superficial radial nerve)**:  Provides cutaneous sensation to the dorsolateral hand, including the dorsal thumb, index finger, and middle finger ((Figure 12)). # Clinically significant tunnels and spaces ## Carpal tunnel The carpal tunnel is a narrow, osteofibrous canal at the volar aspect of the wrist ((Figure 13)). - **Boundaries** - Dorsally and laterally by the carpal bones, which form an arch. - Volarly by the flexor retinaculum (ie, transverse carpal ligament). - Located just distal to the distal wrist crease at the base of the palm. - **Contents** - **Median nerve**:  Passes through the carpal tunnel and lies superficial (volar) to the flexor tendons within the tunnel; it is most vulnerable to compression at this site. - **Flexor tendons** (9):  Four from FDS, 4 from FDP, and 1 from FPL. - **Clinical significance** - Compression of the median nerve leads to **carpal tunnel syndrome**, presenting with numbness, tingling, and burning in the radial 3½ digits.  Symptoms are typically worsened at night or with wrist flexion. - Chronic compression causes thenar muscle atrophy, weakness of thumb opposition, and impaired fine motor skills. ((Figure 14)), ((Figure 15)). ## Guyon canal This fibroosseous tunnel on the ulnar side of the volar wrist is positioned superficially and ulnarly to the carpal tunnel ((Figure 16)). - **Boundaries** - Ulnar side:  Pisiform. - Radial side:  Hook of the hamate. - Floor:  Transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum). - Roof:  Volar carpal ligament and pisohamate ligament. - **Contents** - **Ulnar nerve**:  Divides within the canal into a superficial sensory branch and a deep motor branch. - **Ulnar artery**:  Runs alongside the nerve. - **Clinical significance** - Compression of the ulnar nerve in Guyon canal (ie, **Guyon canal syndrome**) causes sensory loss in the ulnar digits and/or intrinsic hand muscle weakness, depending on the compression zone. - Dorsal ulnar sensation remains intact because the dorsal cutaneous branch exits proximal to the canal. ## Anatomic snuffbox This shallow, triangular depression at the dorsoradial wrist is defined by the following borders.  It is an anatomic space, not a true compartment or tunnel ((Figure 17)). - **Boundaries** - Medial:  Tendon of the extensor pollicis longus. - Lateral:  Tendons of the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB). - Proximal:  Styloid process of the radius. - Floor:  Scaphoid and trapezium bones. - **Contents** - **Radial artery**:  Main vascular structure crossing the floor. - **Superficial branch of the radial nerve**:  Courses superficially over the region. - **Cephalic vein**:  Runs subcutaneously across the roof. - **Clinical relevance** - Tenderness in the snuffbox is a sign of **scaphoid fracture** ((Figure 18)). - The main blood supply to the scaphoid is provided by the dorsal scaphoid branch of the radial artery; this branch enters near the bone's distal pole and then proceeds in a retrograde manner to provide blood supply to the proximal pole.  Because fracture of the scaphoid can easily interrupt this retrograde flow, the fractured scaphoid is at risk for avascular necrosis of the proximal pole and fracture nonunion ((Figure 19)). # Additional clinical correlations ## De Quervain tenosynovitis De Quervain tenosynovitis involves stenosing inflammation of the first dorsal compartment, which houses the APL and EPB tendons.  Thickening of the tendon sheath restricts normal gliding, producing pain over the radial styloid that worsens with thumb motion and ulnar deviation of the wrist.  Chronic inflammation can lead to persistent tendon entrapment and impaired thumb abduction and extension.  The condition is often confirmed with a Finkelstein or Eichhoff test, in which ulnar deviation of the wrist reproduces the patient's radial-sided pain.  The two tests are similar and often confused.  The Finkelstein test involves the examiner passively deviating the wrist ulnarly while the patient's thumb is held out.  The Eichhoff test places the thumb inside a closed fist before ulnar deviation, which increases strain on the APL and EPB.  The "Finkelstein test" is the term most commonly used in practice and is often used to describe both maneuvers ((Figure 20)), ((Video 1)). ## Lunate dislocation Lunate dislocation requires a high-energy force to disrupt the numerous ligaments (eg, scapholunate, capitolunate, lunotriquetral) that typically stabilize the lunate.  When severe ligamentous injury occurs, the lunate can dislocate volarly from its normal position, compressing and/or injuring the median nerve.  Prompt reduction of the dislocated lunate is required to prevent permanent damage to the median nerve ((Figure 21)), ((Figure 22)). ## Scapholunate ligament injury The SLIL stabilizes the scaphoid and lunate.  Disruption of this ligament causes the scaphoid to flex and the lunate to extend, widening the scapholunate gap and producing instability.  Chronic injury alters carpal mechanics and can progress to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC wrist) with degenerative arthritis. ## Triangular fibrocartilage complex injury The TFCC stabilizes the distal DRUJ and ulnar carpus.  Injury causes DRUJ instability and abnormal pronation-supination motion.  It presents with ulnar-sided wrist pain, clicking, or grip weakness.  Chronic disruption alters load transmission across the ulnocarpal joint and may contribute to degenerative changes. ​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌
